Learning Quantum Matter through Attention in Complex Space

Abstract

Magnetic many-electron wavefunctions require amplitude and phase to be optimized together. Whether a complex internal representation improves this variational search is a practical question for neural wavefunction design. We introduce Complex Psiformer for interacting electrons in a magnetic moiré continuum, combining complex hidden features and Hermitian-magnitude attention with magnetic boundary conditions and fermionic antisymmetry. After the same number of optimization steps, Complex Psiformer reaches lower energies than Real Psiformer in two finite supercells. Both Psiformers also improve on their respective neural Hartree–Fock references. Across five training seeds in the 2525-cell system, the mean Complex advantage is 1.458​meV1.458\,\mathrm{meV} per electron, with a smaller observed spread. A separately trained two-electron Complex state has a smaller energy gap to a finite configuration-interaction reference than its Real counterpart. In the Complex states, flux scans show nonmonotonic density correlations and weaker honeycomb mean-density modulation at higher flux, while connected fluctuations persist. Gauge-invariant current maps provide a qualitative comparison of local circulation in the optimized states. These benchmarks support the combined architecture as a variational ansatz for studying energies and charge arrangements in finite magnetic systems.

I Introduction

Variational descriptions of interacting electrons in a perpendicular magnetic field must account for strong electronic correlations and the configuration-dependent phase of the many-body wavefunction. In a periodic supercell, fermionic antisymmetry must be combined with gauge-dependent boundary transition phases [17, 34]. Enforcing these boundary conditions leaves the many-body amplitude and phase within the cell to be optimized. The phase gradients contribute to the covariant kinetic energy and determine local currents together with the amplitude and vector potential. Moiré superlattices bring this problem to experimentally accessible fields, where commensurate charge order and Hofstadter states compete as the flux per moiré cell varies [8, 23].

First-quantized fermionic wavefunctions conventionally enforce antisymmetry through Slater determinants and describe correlations with Jastrow factors, backflow transformations, or multideterminant expansions [12, 29]. Neural quantum states introduce trainable representations optimized by variational Monte Carlo (VMC) [4, 7]. Early studies established the use of neural-network representations for fermionic many-body states [3]. SlaterNet learns one-electron orbitals, while FermiNet and PauliNet construct orbitals that depend on the electronic configuration [39, 18]. Attention-based architectures introduce this dependence by exchanging information between electron streams before determinant projection [16, 48]. These approaches have produced accurate results for molecules, periodic solids, moiré materials, and quantum Hall systems [37, 27, 49, 45].

Several first-quantized ansatzes describe complex wavefunctions using real hidden features together with complex orbital readouts or additional complex-valued factors [16, 45, 36, 1]. In the Real Psiformer baseline considered here, attention exchanges real-valued features before the orbital readout forms complex coefficients. Organizing hidden electron features as complex amplitudes gives radial nonlinearities and Hermitian overlaps a direct role in information exchange before orbital construction. Can the complex structure of quantum mechanics guide a more effective variational search for magnetic many-electron states from first principles?

In this manuscript, we introduce Complex Psiformer for interacting electrons in a magnetic moiré continuum. Here, first-principles means direct variational optimization of the specified effective continuum Hamiltonian. Each orbital combines a fixed section carrying the magnetic boundary transition law with a learned periodic configuration-dependent coefficient. The coefficient network uses reciprocal-lattice phasors, signed radial activations, and Hermitian-magnitude complex-value attention (HMCVA). We adapt this complex attention pattern to electron streams [9], using real attention weights to aggregate complex-valued messages. The resulting orbitals form Slater determinants that enforce fermionic antisymmetry. We also define Complex SlaterNet as an attention-free reference with the same complex orbital construction. The main comparisons use minimum-step stochastic reconfiguration (MinSR) [6, 42] for variational optimization.

We evaluate the complete Complex Psiformer architecture against Real Psiformer and real and complex neural Hartree–Fock (HF) baselines in two finite magnetic supercells. Both Psiformers lower the energies relative to their respective neural HF baselines. After the same number of optimization steps, Complex Psiformer further lowers the mean energy by 1.46​meV1.46\,\mathrm{meV} per electron relative to Real Psiformer over all five attempted training seeds in the 2525-cell system. A separately trained N=2N=2 Complex state also has a smaller energy gap to a finite configuration-interaction reference than its Real counterpart. In the 1818-cell system, the clearer honeycomb-type charge pattern of Complex Psiformer at nϕ=2n_{\phi}=2 is reflected mainly in the mean-density contribution to the structure factor. A flux scan reveals a nonmonotonic redistribution of density correlations. Gauge-invariant current maps show the accompanying local circulation qualitatively.

II Magnetic moiré model and neural wavefunctions

The continuum Hamiltonian and magnetic boundary conditions define the finite-supercell problem. Complex one-particle orbitals form Complex SlaterNet, and attention between electron streams extends it to Complex Psiformer. Section III describes the VMC sampling and optimization procedure.

II.1 Magnetic moiré continuum

We consider an interacting two-dimensional electron gas in a triangular moiré potential under a uniform perpendicular magnetic field. At zero field, the Hamiltonian reduces to the standard effective-mass continuum model for spin-polarized carriers in two-dimensional moiré semiconductors [50, 52, 30, 16]. This model describes aligned transition-metal dichalcogenide (TMD) heterobilayers such as WSe2/WS2\mathrm{WSe}_{2}/\mathrm{WS}_{2}, in which Mott and generalized Wigner-crystal states have been observed at integer and fractional moiré fillings [41]. We work directly in the continuum without projecting onto moiré bands or Landau levels.

The triangular moiré lattice is generated by 𝒂1=aM​(1,0)\bm{a}_{1}=a_{\mathrm{M}}(1,0) and 𝒂2=aM​(1/2,3/2)\bm{a}_{2}=a_{\mathrm{M}}(1/2,\sqrt{3}/2), where aMa_{\mathrm{M}} is the moiré lattice constant. The reciprocal vectors 𝒈1\bm{g}_{1} and 𝒈2\bm{g}_{2} are defined by 𝒈a⋅𝒂b=2​π​δa​b\bm{g}_{a}\cdot\bm{a}_{b}=2\pi\delta_{ab}, and 𝒈3=−(𝒈1+𝒈2)\bm{g}_{3}=-(\bm{g}_{1}+\bm{g}_{2}). The three 𝒈a\bm{g}_{a} are related by 120∘120^{\circ} rotations. Together with their negatives they form the first star of the moiré reciprocal lattice. Keeping this first star gives the standard leading-harmonic potential

VM(𝒓)=−2V0∑a=13cos(𝒈a⋅𝒓+φ),V_{\mathrm{M}}(\bm{r})=-2V_{0}\sum_{a=1}^{3}\cos(\bm{g}_{a}\cdot\bm{r}+\varphi), (1)

used in continuum descriptions of triangular TMD moiré systems [50, 52, 16]. Reality and threefold rotation symmetry reduce the first-star Fourier coefficients to a common amplitude V0V_{0} and a single moiré phase φ\varphi. This phase sets the relative energies of high-symmetry stacking regions and thereby shapes the potential landscape. It is unrelated to the phase of the variational wavefunction. Calculations are performed in an n1×n2n_{1}\times n_{2} periodic supercell, with n1,n2∈ℕ>0n_{1},n_{2}\in\mathbb{N}_{>0}, 𝑳1=n1​𝒂1\bm{L}_{1}=n_{1}\bm{a}_{1}, 𝑳2=n2​𝒂2\bm{L}_{2}=n_{2}\bm{a}_{2}, and area Ω=|𝑳1×𝑳2|>0\Omega=|\bm{L}_{1}\times\bm{L}_{2}|>0. The corresponding reciprocal vectors are 𝑮1=𝒈1/n1\bm{G}_{1}=\bm{g}_{1}/n_{1} and 𝑮2=𝒈2/n2\bm{G}_{2}=\bm{g}_{2}/n_{2}, and hence 𝑮a⋅𝑳b=2​π​δa​b\bm{G}_{a}\cdot\bm{L}_{b}=2\pi\delta_{ab}. The vectors 𝒈a\bm{g}_{a} define the physical moiré potential, whereas 𝑮a\bm{G}_{a} define features that are periodic over the finite simulation cell. We now apply a uniform field 𝑩=B​𝒛^\bm{B}=B\hat{\bm{z}} perpendicular to the plane. Identifying opposite edges of the finite cell makes its geometry a torus, so a consistent magnetic boundary condition requires an integer number of flux quanta through the cell. In the effective atomic units used here,

B​Ω=2​π​nϕ,nϕ∈ℤ≥0.B\Omega=2\pi n_{\phi},\quad n_{\phi}\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}. (2)

Thus nϕn_{\phi} is the number of flux quanta through the supercell. At nϕ=0n_{\phi}=0, the field vanishes, the magnetic section is not applied, and the wavefunction obeys ordinary periodic boundary conditions. The system is illustrated in Figure 1.

We introduce the field through minimal coupling to a vector potential satisfying (∇×𝑨)z=B(\bm{\nabla}\times\bm{A})_{z}=B. We use the symmetric gauge centered at 𝒍=(lx,ly)=(𝑳1+𝑳2)/2\bm{l}=(l_{x},l_{y})=(\bm{L}_{1}+\bm{L}_{2})/2, for which 𝑨⁡(𝒓)=B⁡(−(y−ly),x−lx)/2\bm{A}(\bm{r})=B(-(y-l_{y}),x-l_{x})/2. Choosing the center of the finite cell as 𝒍\bm{l} is convenient but does not change the magnetic field or any observable. The carrier-charge sign is absorbed into the charge-weighted vector potential, and the finite-field calculations use B>0B>0 in the convention of Equation (3).

Writing the Hamiltonian in effective atomic units, whose material-dependent conversion is given at the beginning of Sec. IV, we obtain

H^=12​∑i=1N(−i​∇i−𝑨⁡(𝒓i))2+∑i=1NVM​(𝒓i)+∑i<jvEw(𝒓i−𝒓j)+N2ξM.\begin{multlined}\hat{H}=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\bigl(-\mathrm{i}\bm{\nabla}_{i}-\bm{A}(\bm{r}_{i})\bigr)^{2}+\sum_{i=1}^{N}V_{\mathrm{M}}(\bm{r}_{i})\\ +\sum_{i<j}v_{\mathrm{Ew}}(\bm{r}_{i}-\bm{r}_{j})+\frac{N}{2}\xi_{\mathrm{M}}.\end{multlined} (3)

Here NN is the number of electrons, and ∇i\bm{\nabla}_{i} differentiates with respect to the coordinate 𝒓i\bm{r}_{i}. The first two terms describe the minimally coupled kinetic energy and the moiré potential. We evaluate the Coulomb interaction in the periodically repeated supercell using the two-dimensional Ewald form. The periodic pair interaction vEwv_{\mathrm{Ew}} includes the neutralizing-background correction, while ξM\xi_{\mathrm{M}} is the Madelung self-energy. Together, these contributions give the full Coulomb energy [13, 12, 16]. Their explicit forms are given in Appendix B.

The symmetric-gauge vector potential is not periodic. Under a supercell translation, it changes by the gauge transformation 𝑨⁡(𝒓+𝑳a)=𝑨⁡(𝒓)+∇Λa​(𝒓)\bm{A}(\bm{r}+\bm{L}_{a})=\bm{A}(\bm{r})+\bm{\nabla}\Lambda_{a}(\bm{r}), where Λa​(𝒓)=B​[𝑳a×(𝒓−𝒍)]z/2\Lambda_{a}(\bm{r})=B[\bm{L}_{a}\times(\bm{r}-\bm{l})]_{z}/2. Gauge covariance of the kinetic energy therefore fixes the magnetic boundary condition.

Ψ⁡(…,𝒓i+𝑳a,…)=ei​Λa​(𝒓i)​Ψ​(…,𝒓i,…).\Psi(\ldots,\bm{r}_{i}+\bm{L}_{a},\ldots)=e^{\mathrm{i}\Lambda_{a}(\bm{r}_{i})}\Psi(\ldots,\bm{r}_{i},\ldots). (4)

The vector potential fixes the gauge-transition phase ei​Λa​(𝒓)e^{\mathrm{i}\Lambda_{a}(\bm{r})}. It contains no variational parameter or additional boundary twist. Translating the same electron by 𝑳1\bm{L}_{1} and 𝑳2\bm{L}_{2} in opposite orders yields the relative phase e−i​B​Ωe^{-\mathrm{i}B\Omega}. Equation (2) sets this phase to unity and ensures that the two magnetic boundary identifications are consistent [34, 17]. In the neural wavefunctions below, the learned coefficients remain periodic over the supercell. Fixed single-particle functions supply the magnetic translation law in Equation (4).

II.2 Neural-wavefunction hierarchy

Following Ref. [16], we combine a periodic neural coefficient with the magnetic boundary structure of a single-particle orbital. Applying this construction independently to every electron gives Complex SlaterNet. HMCVA then couples the electron representations and produces the configuration-dependent orbitals of Complex Psiformer. Figure 2 summarizes both architectures. Appendix A places them in the broader context of variational fermionic wavefunctions.

II.3 From plane waves to one-body orbitals

We construct each neural orbital from a coordinate feature, a feed-forward network, and a scalar readout. The first step maps the coordinate to a complex feature vector. For a periodic supercell, we choose a finite set {𝑲μ}μ=1df\{\bm{K}_{\mu}\}_{\mu=1}^{d_{f}} of supercell reciprocal-lattice vectors. Each vector satisfies 𝑲μ⋅𝑳∈2​π​ℤ\bm{K}_{\mu}\cdot\bm{L}\in 2\pi\mathbb{Z} for every supercell translation 𝑳\bm{L}. The feature map is

𝒇0​(𝒓)≡feature⁡(𝒓)=(ei​𝑲1⋅𝒓,…,ei​𝑲df⋅𝒓)∈ℂdf,\bm{f}^{0}(\bm{r})\equiv\operatorname{feature}(\bm{r})=\left(e^{\mathrm{i}\bm{K}_{1}\cdot\bm{r}},\ldots,e^{\mathrm{i}\bm{K}_{d_{f}}\cdot\bm{r}}\right)\in\mathbb{C}^{d_{f}}, (5)

where dfd_{f} is the number of selected modes and need not equal the spatial dimension dd. The set may contain fundamental modes, higher harmonics, or other reciprocal-lattice combinations. Every component of 𝒇0\bm{f}^{0} is continuous and periodic under supercell translations. Complex phasors contain the same information as the paired sine and cosine coordinates used in Refs. [37, 5, 16]. These inputs respect supercell translation symmetry. Each ei​𝑲μ⋅𝒓e^{\mathrm{i}\bm{K}_{\mu}\cdot\bm{r}} is a plane-wave basis function for periodic functions. The nonlinear network nevertheless uses the selected modes as features and does not restrict the orbital to their linear span. Our calculations use the two-dimensional specialization 𝑲1,𝑲2=𝑮1,𝑮2{\bm{K}_{1},\bm{K}_{2}}={\bm{G}_{1},\bm{G}_{2}} and df=2d_{f}=2. The phasor arguments encode periodic position rather than the phase of the many-body wavefunction.

Second, a bias-free embedding maps the coordinate feature to the first hidden representation,

𝒉0​(𝒓)=W0​𝒇0​(𝒓)+V0​𝒇0​(𝒓)¯.\bm{h}^{0}(\bm{r})=W^{0}\bm{f}^{0}(\bm{r})+V^{0}\overline{\bm{f}^{0}(\bm{r})}. (6)

Here dLd_{\rm L} is the common hidden-layer width, and W0,V0∈ℂdL×dfW^{0},V^{0}\in\mathbb{C}^{d_{\rm L}\times d_{f}} map the input to 𝒉0∈ℂdL\bm{h}^{0}\in\mathbb{C}^{d_{\rm L}}. The overline denotes componentwise complex conjugation. Because the orbital is a complex-valued function of real coordinates, the embedding need not be holomorphic. The term W0​𝒇0W^{0}\bm{f}^{0} alone defines a complex-linear map. Including V0​𝒇0¯V^{0}\overline{\bm{f}^{0}} gives a general real-linear map between the underlying real vector spaces. For the phasor features in Equation (5), the conjugate channel also provides the opposite reciprocal modes e−i𝑲μ⋅𝒓e^{-\mathrm{i}\bm{K}_{\mu}\cdot\bm{r}}.

The network contains LL residual layers. For l=0,…,L−1l=0,\ldots,L-1, layer l+1l+1 uses the real-affine map

ℱl+1​(𝒛)=Wl+1​𝒛+Vl+1​𝒛¯+𝒃l+1.\mathcal{F}^{l+1}(\bm{z})=W^{l+1}\bm{z}+V^{l+1}\overline{\bm{z}}+\bm{b}^{l+1}. (7)

Here Wl+1,Vl+1∈ℂdL×dLW^{l+1},V^{l+1}\in\mathbb{C}^{d_{\rm L}\times d_{\rm L}} and 𝒃l+1∈ℂdL\bm{b}^{l+1}\in\mathbb{C}^{d_{\rm L}}. The linear part is real-linear, while the bias makes the complete map real-affine. We then apply a signed radial activation to 𝒛∈ℂdL\bm{z}\in\mathbb{C}^{d_{\rm L}}.

σl+1​(𝒛)=tanh⁡(|𝒛|−𝚫l+1)​𝒛|𝒛|.\sigma^{l+1}(\bm{z})=\tanh\left(|\bm{z}|-\bm{\Delta}^{l+1}\right)\frac{\bm{z}}{|\bm{z}|}. (8)

This activation follows amplitude–phase constructions used in complex-valued networks, including the pointwise modReLU activation [19, 2]. We use a signed tanh\tanh response. In numerical calculations, we replace |𝒛||\bm{z}| in the denominator by |𝒛|+10−8|\bm{z}|+10^{-8} to regularize the activation at the origin. All operations in Equation (8) act elementwise. The trainable offsets 𝚫l+1∈ℝdL\bm{\Delta}^{l+1}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\rm L}}, initialized at zero, shift the crossover of the radial response. A negative radial response reverses the channel phase by π\pi. The regularity relevant to energy evaluation is discussed in Appendix E. The complete residual update is 𝒉l+1=𝒉l+σl+1​(ℱl+1​(𝒉l))\bm{h}^{l+1}=\bm{h}^{l}+\sigma^{l+1}(\mathcal{F}^{l+1}(\bm{h}^{l})).

After LL residual layers, a trainable vector 𝒘∈ℂdL\bm{w}\in\mathbb{C}^{d_{\rm L}} produces the periodic neural coefficient 𝒘⋅𝒉L​(𝒓)\bm{w}\cdot\bm{h}^{L}(\bm{r}). At zero field, this coefficient can serve directly as a periodic orbital. In a magnetic field, the orbital must instead acquire the position-dependent transition phase ei​Λa​(𝒓)e^{\mathrm{i}\Lambda_{a}(\bm{r})} in Equation (4) under a supercell translation. We separate this prescribed boundary law from the trainable periodic coefficient by introducing fixed single-particle functions χj\chi_{j} satisfying

χj​(𝒓+𝑳a)=ei​Λa​(𝒓)​χj​(𝒓).\chi_{j}(\bm{r}+\bm{L}_{a})=e^{\mathrm{i}\Lambda_{a}(\bm{r})}\chi_{j}(\bm{r}). (9)

The index jj labels an orbital column in the Slater matrix. In the language of magnetic translations, each χj\chi_{j} is a magnetic section [34]. It is represented within one cell, with opposite edges related by the required gauge-transition phases. These fixed, nontrainable functions contain amplitude and phase structure within the cell and obey the same transition law. Multiplying a periodic neural coefficient by χj\chi_{j} therefore gives an orbital with the correct magnetic boundary condition. The construction of χj\chi_{j} uses torus Landau-type functions. Multiplication by an arbitrary periodic neural coefficient does not, however, restrict the orbital to a fixed Landau-level subspace. Each orbital inherits the zeros of its fixed factor. A zero of one orbital at one electron position need not make the determinant vanish, so these factors alone do not determine the nodes of the full many-electron wavefunction. Appendix C describes the construction of χj\chi_{j}. Every model considered below uses this same factorization, with the fixed magnetic section carrying the prescribed boundary phase factor.

II.4 Complex SlaterNet

Complex SlaterNet constructs an antisymmetric many-electron state by applying the one-body network independently to each electron. Electron ii starts from 𝒇i0=𝒇0​(𝒓i)\bm{f}_{i}^{0}=\bm{f}^{0}(\bm{r}_{i}) and passes through the single-particle stream 𝒉i0,…,𝒉iL\bm{h}_{i}^{0},\ldots,\bm{h}_{i}^{L} described above [16]. All electrons share the embedding and residual-layer parameters. Since the layers do not mix electron streams, the final hidden vector retains the one-body form 𝒉iL=𝒉L​(𝒓i)\bm{h}_{i}^{L}=\bm{h}^{L}(\bm{r}_{i}).

For determinant mm, the element in electron row ii and orbital column jj is

ϕjm​(𝒓i)=χj​(𝒓i)​[𝒘jm⋅𝒉iL​(𝒓i)],\phi_{j}^{m}(\bm{r}_{i})=\chi_{j}(\bm{r}_{i})\bigl[\bm{w}_{j}^{m}\cdot\bm{h}_{i}^{L}(\bm{r}_{i})\bigr], (10)

where 𝒘jm∈ℂdL\bm{w}_{j}^{m}\in\mathbb{C}^{d_{\rm L}}. The orbitals need not be orthogonal, although linearly dependent orbitals make the determinant vanish. With DD determinants, the wavefunction is

Ψ⁡(𝑹)=∑m=1Ddet[ϕjm​(𝒓i)]i,j=1N.\Psi(\bm{R})=\sum_{m=1}^{D}\det\!\left[\phi_{j}^{m}(\bm{r}_{i})\right]_{i,j=1}^{N}. (11)

For D>1D>1, the determinant values are summed directly without independent mixing coefficients, as written in Equation (11). Exchanging two electrons exchanges two rows of every Slater matrix and changes the sign of the wavefunction. Translating electron ii by 𝑳a\bm{L}_{a} leaves the periodic coefficient unchanged. It multiplies every element of row ii by the common phase ei​Λa​(𝒓i)e^{\mathrm{i}\Lambda_{a}(\bm{r}_{i})}. The determinant therefore satisfies the many-body magnetic boundary condition in Equation (4). For D=1D=1, Complex SlaterNet is the neural analogue of an unrestricted single-determinant ansatz. Increasing DD gives a finite multideterminant expansion without changing the one-body dependence in Equation (10). Complex SlaterNet therefore provides the attention-free reference for introducing configuration-dependent orbitals.

II.5 Complex Psiformer wavefunction

Self-attention is central to Transformer architectures [47]. Complex-valued variants use real–imaginary channels, complex projections, or Hermitian-magnitude similarities for sequence and signal data [51, 9, 35]. We adapt this Hermitian-magnitude score and complex-value aggregation pattern to permutation-equivariant electron streams and call the resulting block HMCVA. This existing attention pattern couples the periodic complex coefficients before the determinant, while the fixed magnetic sections enforce the torus transition law.

Complex SlaterNet constructs each orbital value from one electron stream. Following Ref. [16], attention extends this one-body orbital according to ϕjm​(𝒓i)→ϕjm​(𝒓i,{𝒓/i})\phi_{j}^{m}(\bm{r}_{i})\rightarrow\phi_{j}^{m}(\bm{r}_{i};\{\bm{r}_{/i}\}), where {𝒓/i}={𝒓k:k≠i}\{\bm{r}_{/i}\}=\{\bm{r}_{k}:k\neq i\} denotes the positions of all other electrons. The coordinate before the semicolon identifies the electron row, while the coordinates after it describe the many-electron environment. HMCVA makes 𝒉iL\bm{h}_{i}^{L} a permutation-equivariant function of the full configuration. The resulting orbitals carry many-electron dependence, as in neural backflow and self-attention wavefunctions [39, 48, 16].

At each layer, HMCVA exchanges information between electron streams before the residual feed-forward update.

{𝒉il}i=1N→HMCVA{𝒇il+1}i=1N→feed​-​forward{𝒉il+1}i=1N.\{\bm{h}_{i}^{l}\}_{i=1}^{N}\xrightarrow{\mathrm{HMCVA}}\{\bm{f}_{i}^{l+1}\}_{i=1}^{N}\xrightarrow{\mathrm{feed\text{-}forward}}\{\bm{h}_{i}^{l+1}\}_{i=1}^{N}.

We write the attention residual as 𝒇il+1=𝒉il+𝒂il\bm{f}_{i}^{l+1}=\bm{h}_{i}^{l}+\bm{a}_{i}^{l}, where 𝒂il\bm{a}_{i}^{l} is the multi-head update defined below. The feed-forward layer then gives 𝒉il+1=𝒇il+1+σl+1​(ℱl+1​(𝒇il+1))\bm{h}_{i}^{l+1}=\bm{f}_{i}^{l+1}+\sigma^{l+1}(\mathcal{F}^{l+1}(\bm{f}_{i}^{l+1})).

At layer ll, the index h=1,…,Nheadsh=1,\ldots,N_{\rm heads} labels an attention head. Independent bias-free real-linear maps produce a query, a key, and a value for each electron stream.

𝒒il​h=Wql​h​𝒉il+Vql​h​𝒉il¯,𝒌il​h=Wkl​h​𝒉il+Vkl​h​𝒉il¯,𝒗il​h=Wvl​h​𝒉il+Vvl​h​𝒉il¯.\begin{array}[]{rcl}\bm{q}_{i}^{lh}&=&W_{q}^{lh}\bm{h}_{i}^{l}+V_{q}^{lh}\overline{\bm{h}_{i}^{l}},\\ \bm{k}_{i}^{lh}&=&W_{k}^{lh}\bm{h}_{i}^{l}+V_{k}^{lh}\overline{\bm{h}_{i}^{l}},\\ \bm{v}_{i}^{lh}&=&W_{v}^{lh}\bm{h}_{i}^{l}+V_{v}^{lh}\overline{\bm{h}_{i}^{l}}.\end{array} (12)

The query 𝒒il​h∈ℂdq\bm{q}_{i}^{lh}\in\mathbb{C}^{d_{q}} specifies the learned features sought by the receiving stream ii. The key 𝒌jl​h∈ℂdk\bm{k}_{j}^{lh}\in\mathbb{C}^{d_{k}} describes how source stream jj matches that query. The value 𝒗jl​h∈ℂdv\bm{v}_{j}^{lh}\in\mathbb{C}^{d_{v}} carries the complex message from the source. The trainable matrices Wql​h,Vql​hW_{q}^{lh},V_{q}^{lh}, Wkl​h,Vkl​hW_{k}^{lh},V_{k}^{lh}, and Wvl​h,Vvl​hW_{v}^{lh},V_{v}^{lh} have shapes dq×dLd_{q}\times d_{\rm L}, dk×dLd_{k}\times d_{\rm L}, and dv×dLd_{v}\times d_{\rm L}, respectively, over ℂ\mathbb{C}. The query and key share the width dq=dkd_{q}=d_{k}, while dvd_{v} is independent.

HMCVA compares receiver ii with source jj through the magnitude of their Hermitian dot product, scaled by the query width.

si​jl​h=|𝒒il​h¯⋅𝒌jl​h|dq.s_{ij}^{lh}=\frac{|\overline{\bm{q}_{i}^{lh}}\cdot\bm{k}_{j}^{lh}|}{\sqrt{d_{q}}}. (13)

This score measures compatibility in the learned complex query–key space. The absolute value removes the phase of the query–key overlap from the real attention weight. Since the query and key maps are independent, si​jl​hs_{ij}^{lh} need not equal sj​il​hs_{ji}^{lh}. A larger si​jl​hs_{ij}^{lh} gives source jj more influence on the correlated representation of electron ii, relative to the other sources. This internal relevance measure has no direct interpretation as a physical orbital overlap or interaction energy.

A softmax over all source electrons converts the scores into attention weights. These weights then combine the complex values.

αi​jl​h=esi​jl​h∑n=1Nesi​nl​h,HEADil​h=∑j=1Nαi​jl​h​𝒗jl​h.\alpha_{ij}^{lh}=\frac{e^{s_{ij}^{lh}}}{\sum_{n=1}^{N}e^{s_{in}^{lh}}},\qquad\operatorname{HEAD}_{i}^{lh}=\sum_{j=1}^{N}\alpha_{ij}^{lh}\bm{v}_{j}^{lh}. (14)

The weights αi​jl​h\alpha_{ij}^{lh} are real, non-negative, and normalized over jj. They include the self-pair j=ij=i. The weighted sum HEADil​h∈ℂdv\operatorname{HEAD}_{i}^{lh}\in\mathbb{C}^{d_{v}} is the output of head hh for electron ii. Because the weights are real, the output retains the amplitude and phase information carried by the complex values. Appendix D discusses the symmetry consequences of this score.

The NheadsN_{\rm heads} outputs are concatenated in ℂNheads​dv\mathbb{C}^{N_{\rm heads}d_{v}} and mapped back to ℂdL\mathbb{C}^{d_{\rm L}} by a bias-free real-linear output map with Wol,Vol∈ℂdL×(Nheads​dv)W_{\rm o}^{l},V_{\rm o}^{l}\in\mathbb{C}^{d_{\rm L}\times(N_{\rm heads}d_{v})}. The projected output defines the attention update 𝒂il\bm{a}_{i}^{l} used above. All maps are shared across electrons, and the sums over source streams do not depend on their ordering. HMCVA is therefore permutation equivariant. After LL blocks, 𝒉iL​(𝑹)\bm{h}_{i}^{L}(\bm{R}) remains associated with electron ii while depending on the full configuration.

Attention changes the periodic neural coefficient from a one-body function of 𝒓i\bm{r}_{i} to a permutation-equivariant function of the full configuration, while preserving the magnetic orbital structure. Reusing the same fixed χj\chi_{j}, the Complex Psiformer orbital is

ϕjm​(𝒓i,{𝒓/i})=χj​(𝒓i)​[𝒘jm⋅𝒉iL​(𝑹)].\phi_{j}^{m}(\bm{r}_{i};\{\bm{r}_{/i}\})=\chi_{j}(\bm{r}_{i})\bigl[\bm{w}_{j}^{m}\cdot\bm{h}_{i}^{L}(\bm{R})\bigr]. (15)

Equation (15) differs from the Complex SlaterNet orbital in Equation (10) through its second argument. The magnetic factor χj​(𝒓i)\chi_{j}(\bm{r}_{i}) remains one-body, while 𝒉iL​(𝑹)\bm{h}_{i}^{L}(\bm{R}) allows the periodic coefficient to respond to every other electron. Replacing each one-body orbital value in Equation (11) with this correlated orbital gives the Complex Psiformer wavefunction. The shared Slater structure therefore preserves fermionic antisymmetry and the magnetic boundary condition, as shown in Appendix D.

III Variational Monte Carlo

III.1 Variational energy and Monte Carlo sampling

We optimize the real parameters 𝜽∈ℝP\bm{\theta}\in\mathbb{R}^{P} of the complex trial wavefunction Ψ𝜽​(𝑹)\Psi_{\bm{\theta}}(\bm{R}) by variational Monte Carlo (VMC) [12, 16]. During training, Metropolis–Hastings sampling targets the density 𝗉𝜽​(𝑹)∝|Ψ𝜽​(𝑹)|2\mathsf{p}_{\bm{\theta}}(\bm{R})\propto|\Psi_{\bm{\theta}}(\bm{R})|^{2}. At configurations where Ψ𝜽​(𝑹)≠0\Psi_{\bm{\theta}}(\bm{R})\neq 0, the local energy is

Eloc,𝜽​(𝑹)=Ψ𝜽−1​(𝑹)​[H^​Ψ𝜽]​(𝑹).E_{\mathrm{loc},\bm{\theta}}(\bm{R})=\Psi_{\bm{\theta}}^{-1}(\bm{R})[\hat{H}\Psi_{\bm{\theta}}](\bm{R}).

Its expectation gives the variational energy,

E𝜽=𝔼𝑹∼𝗉𝜽​[Eloc,𝜽​(𝑹)].E_{\bm{\theta}}=\mathbb{E}_{\bm{R}\sim\mathsf{p}_{\bm{\theta}}}\left[E_{\mathrm{loc},\bm{\theta}}(\bm{R})\right]. (16)

For a trial state in the operator domain of the self-adjoint Hamiltonian H^\hat{H}, this expectation is real. It bounds the ground-state energy from above, although individual local-energy samples may be complex.

Locally away from nodes, the wavefunction can be written as Ψ𝜽​(𝑹)=eu𝜽​(𝑹)​ei​ϕ𝜽​(𝑹)\Psi_{\bm{\theta}}(\bm{R})=e^{u_{\bm{\theta}}(\bm{R})}e^{\mathrm{i}\phi_{\bm{\theta}}(\bm{R})}, where u𝜽​(𝑹)=log⁡|Ψ𝜽​(𝑹)|u_{\bm{\theta}}(\bm{R})=\log|\Psi_{\bm{\theta}}(\bm{R})| is the log amplitude and ϕ𝜽​(𝑹)\phi_{\bm{\theta}}(\bm{R}) is the local phase. Sampling depends only on u𝜽u_{\bm{\theta}}, while the kinetic local energy requires coordinate derivatives of both u𝜽u_{\bm{\theta}} and ϕ𝜽\phi_{\bm{\theta}}. Although exact nodes carry zero sampling probability, nearby configurations can produce large local-energy fluctuations. The independent Psiformer comparisons use the magnetic quadratic form under the conditions and sampling protocol specified in Appendix E.

III.2 Stochastic reconfiguration and MinSR

All four models use stochastic reconfiguration (SR) [44] through the same minimum-step SR (MinSR) implementation [6, 42].

For a batch {𝑹b}b=1M\{\bm{R}_{b}\}_{b=1}^{M}, we collect the log-amplitude and phase derivatives in Ju,Jϕ∈ℝM×PJ^{u},J^{\phi}\in\mathbb{R}^{M\times P}, with Jb​μu=∂θμu𝜽​(𝑹b)J^{u}_{b\mu}=\partial_{\theta_{\mu}}u_{\bm{\theta}}(\bm{R}_{b}) and Jb​μϕ=∂θμϕ𝜽​(𝑹b)J^{\phi}_{b\mu}=\partial_{\theta_{\mu}}\phi_{\bm{\theta}}(\bm{R}_{b}). Away from nodes and phase-branch discontinuities, they satisfy

Ψ𝜽−1​(𝑹b)​∂θμΨ𝜽​(𝑹b)=Jb​μu+i​Jb​μϕ.\Psi_{\bm{\theta}}^{-1}(\bm{R}_{b})\partial_{\theta_{\mu}}\Psi_{\bm{\theta}}(\bm{R}_{b})=J^{u}_{b\mu}+\mathrm{i}J^{\phi}_{b\mu}. (17)

For a differentiable trial family in the operator domain, the energy gradient is a covariance of these responses with the local energy. This expression assumes a parameter-independent Hamiltonian, as derived in Appendix E. The centered amplitude and phase responses couple to the real and imaginary local-energy residuals, respectively.

For a batch of MM configurations, we stack the centered amplitude and phase Jacobians into one real matrix,

X=1M​(Ju−J¯uJϕ−J¯ϕ)∈ℝ2​M×P.X=\frac{1}{\sqrt{M}}\begin{pmatrix}J^{u}-\overline{J}^{u}\\ J^{\phi}-\overline{J}^{\phi}\end{pmatrix}\in\mathbb{R}^{2M\times P}. (18)

Here the bars denote column-wise batch means. The vector 𝒚∈ℝ2​M\bm{y}\in\mathbb{R}^{2M} stacks the centered real and imaginary local-energy residuals with the same M−1/2M^{-1/2} scaling. The MinSR parameter update is

Δ​𝜽=−2​η​X𝖳​(X​X𝖳+λ​I)−1​𝒚,\Delta\bm{\theta}=-2\eta X^{\mathsf{T}}(XX^{\mathsf{T}}+\lambda I)^{-1}\bm{y}, (19)

where η\eta is the learning rate, λ\lambda is the damping, and II is the identity in sample space. The linear solve has dimension 2​M2M instead of PP. In training, energy clipping and an SR-metric norm constraint modify the update, as detailed in Appendix E. We use Kronecker-factored approximate-curvature (KFAC) optimization only for the auxiliary comparison in that appendix [32, 39]. Network and optimization settings are listed in Tables 3, 4, and 5.

IV Main results

We study N=12N=12 electrons in a fixed spin-polarized sector, including the periodic Ewald interaction and its Madelung term. The 2525-cell system uses a 5×55\times 5 moiré supercell, while the 1818-cell system uses a 3×63\times 6 supercell. Their electron fillings per moiré cell are 12/2512/25 and 2/32/3, respectively. Both benchmarks have nϕ=2n_{\phi}=2 and use the cell-centered symmetric gauge and magnetic boundary conditions defined in Section II.1. They differ in both electron filling and flux density, so they do not form a fixed-density finite-size sequence. The zero-field member of the flux scan uses ordinary periodic boundary conditions.

We use the WSe2/WS2\mathrm{WSe}_{2}/\mathrm{WS}_{2} continuum-model parameters of Ref. [16]. They are m∗/me=0.35m^{*}/m_{e}=0.35, V0=15​meVV_{0}=15\,\mathrm{meV}, φ=π/4\varphi=\pi/4, aM=8.031​nma_{\mathrm{M}}=8.031\,\mathrm{nm}, and ϵ=5.0\epsilon=5.0. Length and energy are measured in the effective Bohr radius and Hartree, respectively, with aB∗=ϵ​mem∗​aBa_{B}^{*}=\frac{\epsilon m_{e}}{m^{*}}a_{B} and Ha∗=m∗me​ϵ2​Ha\mathrm{Ha}^{*}=\frac{m^{*}}{m_{e}\epsilon^{2}}\mathrm{Ha}.

For aM=8.031​nma_{\mathrm{M}}=8.031\,\mathrm{nm}, the moiré unit-cell area is 55.9​nm255.9\,\mathrm{nm}^{2}. The 2525- and 1818-cell benchmarks contain 0.0800.080 and 0.1110.111 flux quanta per moiré cell. These values correspond to laboratory fields of approximately 5.95.9 and 8.2​T8.2\,\mathrm{T}, respectively. The nϕ=0,…,4n_{\phi}=0,\ldots,4 scan of the 1818-cell system spans zero field and finite fields from approximately 4.14.1 to 16.5​T16.5\,\mathrm{T}. Comparable fields have been used to study competing charge-ordered and Hofstadter states in twisted WSe2/MoSe2\mathrm{WSe}_{2}/\mathrm{MoSe}_{2} [23]. The material and filling differ, so this comparison provides physical context rather than a direct experimental benchmark.

Both finite-field benchmarks have N/nϕ=6N/n_{\phi}=6, the number of electrons per magnetic flux quantum. This continuum Landau-level filling differs from the electron filling per moiré cell given above. The cyclotron scales are about 2.0​meV2.0\,\mathrm{meV} at 5.9​T5.9\,\mathrm{T} and 2.7​meV2.7\,\mathrm{meV} at 8.2​T8.2\,\mathrm{T}, both below V0=15​meVV_{0}=15\,\mathrm{meV}. The moiré potential thus remains important alongside magnetic quantization, placing these calculations in a moiré–Hofstadter regime.

IV.1 Variational energy benchmark

We compare the variational energies of Real and Complex Psiformers with each other and with single-determinant neural Hartree–Fock (HF) baselines. The Real and Complex D=1D=1 SlaterNets use configuration-independent orbitals and provide the neural HF baselines. Their finite neural parameterization and optimization need not attain the HF minimum. Energy lowering relative to these baselines assesses the benefit of the more flexible many-electron ansatz, whereas the direct Psiformer comparison assesses the two complete architectures.

We compare the D=4D=4 Real and Complex Psiformers at the same network depth, hidden real dimension, determinant count, MinSR schedule, and 10,000-step optimization budget. Their activations and attention rules remain model specific, and Complex Psiformer has slightly fewer trainable parameters. Both architectures produce complex wavefunctions. Their structural differences and training settings are detailed in Appendices A and F.

Figure 3 shows the training diagnostics. Table 1 reports conventional local-energy estimates as total energies in Ha∗\mathrm{Ha}^{*}. We express the energy reductions below in meV per electron. Complex SlaterNet has the lower mean estimate of the two neural HF baselines in both supercells. Using this lower HF estimate as the common reference, the energy reductions are 3.0793.079 and 0.508​meV0.508\,\mathrm{meV} per electron for Real Psiformer in the 1818- and 2525-cell systems, respectively, and 5.0165.016 and 3.524​meV3.524\,\mathrm{meV} per electron for Complex Psiformer. The additional variational flexibility comes from configuration-dependent orbitals and the four-determinant expansion, as discussed in Appendix A.2.

To assess sensitivity to initialization, we trained each Psiformer with five seeds in the 2525-cell system under the same 10,000-step budget. We then fixed the trained parameters and evaluated each state with a separate Monte Carlo calculation, following the common protocol in Appendix E. Across all five attempts, the mean energies are −48.827-48.827 and −47.369​meV-47.369\,\mathrm{meV} per electron for Complex and Real Psiformer, respectively. Complex Psiformer is lower by 1.458​meV1.458\,\mathrm{meV} per electron on average and in four of the five comparisons by seed index. The sample standard deviations across training seeds are 0.4150.415 and 1.000​meV1.000\,\mathrm{meV} per electron, respectively.

As a controlled small-system comparison, we also optimized the 1818-cell, N=2N=2, nϕ=2n_{\phi}=2 problem and constructed a finite configuration-interaction (CI) reference using 40 active orbitals and all 780 determinants. The CI energy is −0.182​Ha∗-0.182\,\mathrm{Ha}^{*} in total, or −34.675​meV-34.675\,\mathrm{meV} per electron. The frozen Complex and Real endpoints lie 5.7085.708 and 22.599​meV22.599\,\mathrm{meV} per electron above that reference, respectively. Thus the Complex endpoint is 16.891​meV16.891\,\mathrm{meV} per electron below the Real endpoint for this fixed training pair. The energy comparison and its sensitivity to the evaluation sampling distribution are shown in appendix Figure 9. Appendix E.3 gives the reference construction and cutoff checks. The CI result is a controlled finite-basis reference, not an exact continuum energy.

The energy gains apply to the complete Complex Psiformer at the tested settings. Isolating the contributions of the radial activation, attention rule, and residual stabilization requires component comparisons with comparable tuning budgets.

IV.2 Spatial density profiles

The one-body density ρ⁡(𝒓)\rho(\bm{r}) describes the charge distribution within each supercell. It satisfies ∫Ωρ⁡(𝒓)​d2​𝒓=N\int_{\Omega}\rho(\bm{r})\,d^{2}\bm{r}=N, and its spatial mean is ⟨ρ⟩=N/Ω\langle\rho\rangle=N/\Omega. We plot ρ/⟨ρ⟩\rho/\langle\rho\rangle, so that unity denotes a uniform state and deviations from unity measure spatial charge modulation. Figure 4 compares the unaligned Real and Complex Psiformer profiles in the physical parallelogram geometry. At the 1818-cell filling N/(n1​n2)=2/3N/(n_{1}n_{2})=2/3, scanning tunnelling microscopy in WSe2/WS2\mathrm{WSe}_{2}/\mathrm{WS}_{2} has resolved a honeycomb generalized Wigner crystal with two of the three triangular-lattice sublattices occupied [25]. The same charge pattern appears in zero-field continuum calculations with our material parameters and ϵ=5\epsilon=5 [16]. An independent neural-wavefunction study also finds a C3C_{3}-symmetric crystal at this filling [28].

At the main benchmark flux nϕ=2n_{\phi}=2, Complex Psiformer exhibits a clearer honeycomb-type charge arrangement than Real Psiformer [Figure 4(b,e)]. Integrating the density over the nearest-well regions and averaging within the three sublattices gives occupations (0.953,0.157,0.890)(0.953,0.157,0.890) for Complex and (0.933,0.576,0.491)(0.933,0.576,0.491) for Real Psiformer, in the same sublattice convention. The two highly occupied sublattices and one depleted sublattice of the Complex state are closer to the ideal honeycomb motif (1,0,1)(1,0,1). The sublattice construction and the site-resolved comparison are specified in Appendix G. At this flux, the lower-energy Complex state is also closer to the honeycomb pattern identified in the literature. This comparison is qualitative because the cited studies do not provide a ground-state density at the present field of approximately 8.2​T8.2\,\mathrm{T}.

In the Complex states, the honeycomb pattern is clearest at nϕ=2n_{\phi}=2 and weakens at nϕ=4n_{\phi}=4, although local density maxima persist [Figure 4 and Appendix G]. In the fixed spin-polarized model, the field acts through orbital motion and may change which charge arrangement best balances kinetic, moiré-potential, and Coulomb energies. This offers a possible explanation for the reduced honeycomb contrast, although the separate energy contributions have not been compared. Field-dependent competition between charge order and Hofstadter states has also been observed in semiconductor moiré lattices in other filling and band regimes [23]. The field response depends on the regime, as magnetic fields can also stabilize Wigner crystals at low Landau-level filling [46]. For these independently optimized finite-cell states, a loss of honeycomb contrast does not by itself establish crystal melting.

In the 2525-cell system, the density anisotropy varies substantially across the five training seeds (Appendix G). The seeds show no consistent distinction between stripe-like Real states and two-dimensional Complex states. This system has filling 12/2512/25, and its cell geometry is incommensurate with the KK and MM stars. Stripe order is itself observed in the experimental half-filled crystal [25], so a stripe-like density alone does not indicate an unphysical state.

IV.3 Gauge-invariant current flow

The one-body density depends only on the wavefunction amplitude, whereas the gauge-invariant mechanical one-body current probes its phase gradient. At fixed amplitude and vector potential, a change in the many-body phase can modify the current while leaving the density unchanged. We evaluate this current for the frozen 1818-cell, N=12N=12, nϕ=2n_{\phi}=2 checkpoints. Using the local phase ϕ𝜽​(𝑹)\phi_{\bm{\theta}}(\bm{R}) defined above, the particle-current density in effective atomic units is

𝒋⁡(𝒓)=⟨∑i=1NδP​(𝒓−𝒓i)​[∇iϕ𝜽​(𝑹)−𝑨⁡(𝒓i)]⟩|Ψ𝜽|2.\bm{j}(\bm{r})=\left\langle\sum_{i=1}^{N}\delta_{\mathrm{P}}(\bm{r}-\bm{r}_{i})\left[\bm{\nabla}_{i}\phi_{\bm{\theta}}(\bm{R})-\bm{A}(\bm{r}_{i})\right]\right\rangle_{|\Psi_{\bm{\theta}}|^{2}}. (20)

Here δP\delta_{\mathrm{P}} is the periodic delta function, and 𝑨\bm{A} is the cell-centered symmetric-gauge vector potential used in the Hamiltonian. Under a gauge transformation, the change in the phase gradient cancels that in the vector potential, leaving Equation (20) unchanged. Real Psiformer also produces a complex wavefunction from its real hidden features through a complex orbital readout. Both models include the prescribed magnetic section, so the current probes the full optimized phase rather than the boundary factor alone. An exact stationary state also satisfies ∇⋅𝒋=0\bm{\nabla}\cdot\bm{j}=0. This condition permits local circulation without a change in the density. Testing this continuity condition in a variational state requires estimates over the full supercell with sampling uncertainties.

Figure 5 compares the two current fields after 10,00010{,}000 optimization steps, using the same spatial grid, display scales, and window near a selected density maximum. The two fields differ in direction and magnitude near this maximum, with a clearer clockwise circulation in the displayed Complex state. These maps give a qualitative view of local circulation, which depends on both the probability weights and phase gradients in Equation (20). Assessing current or phase accuracy requires an independent reference. Transport and Hall responses require separate response calculations.

IV.4 Flux-dependent density correlations

We examine the flux dependence of density correlations in the 1818-cell Complex Psiformer states optimized independently at nϕ=0,…,4n_{\phi}=0,\ldots,4. The static structure factor resolves their equal-time density correlations in momentum space,

Snϕ​(𝒒)=1N​⟨|∑j=1Nei​𝒒⋅𝒓j|2⟩nϕ.S_{n_{\phi}}(\bm{q})=\frac{1}{N}\left\langle\left|\sum_{j=1}^{N}e^{\mathrm{i}\bm{q}\cdot\bm{r}_{j}}\right|^{2}\right\rangle_{n_{\phi}}. (21)

The average is taken over the optimized state at each flux, with 𝒒=m1​𝑮1+m2​𝑮2\bm{q}=m_{1}\bm{G}_{1}+m_{2}\bm{G}_{2}, m1,m2∈ℤm_{1},m_{2}\in\mathbb{Z}, chosen from the supercell reciprocal lattice defined in Section II.1. Like the one-body density, S⁡(𝒒)S(\bm{q}) depends on |Ψ|2|\Psi|^{2}, but it also resolves correlations between electron positions. Using the independently optimized zero-field state as a reference, we define

Δ​Snϕ​(𝒒)=Snϕ​(𝒒)−S0​(𝒒).\Delta S_{n_{\phi}}(\bm{q})=S_{n_{\phi}}(\bm{q})-S_{0}(\bm{q}). (22)

Figure 6 shows changes concentrated at selected reciprocal-space points, with both positive and negative contributions relative to zero field. Different flux sectors emphasize different modes, with the largest changes visible at nϕ=2n_{\phi}=2 and 44. The magnitudes vary nonmonotonically with flux.

We separate this redistribution into changes in the average charge arrangement and changes in density fluctuations. With ρ𝒒=∑jei​𝒒⋅𝒓j\rho_{\bm{q}}=\sum_{j}e^{\mathrm{i}\bm{q}\cdot\bm{r}_{j}} denoting the dimensionless Fourier component of the microscopic number density, we write

S⁡(𝒒)=|⟨ρ𝒒⟩|2N+⟨|ρ𝒒|2⟩−|⟨ρ𝒒⟩|2N,S(\bm{q})=\frac{|\langle\rho_{\bm{q}}\rangle|^{2}}{N}+\frac{\langle|\rho_{\bm{q}}|^{2}\rangle-|\langle\rho_{\bm{q}}\rangle|^{2}}{N}, (23)

where the first term, denoted by Sdisc​(𝒒)S_{\rm disc}(\bm{q}), is the disconnected contribution from the mean density modulation, and the second term, Sconn​(𝒒)S_{\rm conn}(\bm{q}), describes connected density fluctuations about that mean. This density covariance can also be nonzero in a single Slater determinant. Both contribute to the changes displayed in Figure 6.

We quantify these contributions in an independent evaluation of both Psiformers, averaging over the six moiré Brillouin-zone corners associated with three-sublattice order. The resulting S⁡(K)S(K), Sdisc​(K)S_{\rm disc}(K), and Sconn​(K)S_{\rm conn}(K) are shown in Figure 7. Appendix G specifies the reciprocal vectors and the averaging procedure. At nϕ=2n_{\phi}=2, approximately 95.758%95.758\% of the Complex–Real difference in S⁡(K)S(K) comes from the mean-density contribution, consistent with the clearer honeycomb arrangement in Figure 4(b). In the Complex states, this contribution becomes small at nϕ=4n_{\phi}=4, while the connected component remains finite and increases from its value at nϕ=2n_{\phi}=2. The decrease in S⁡(K)S(K) is therefore dominated by the loss of its mean-density contribution, despite the increase in connected fluctuations. Averaging over translated charge arrangements can also weaken the mean-density pattern while retaining crystalline correlations, as discussed in Appendix G.

Each point represents one independently optimized training endpoint. The error bars in Figure 7 describe sampling of these fixed states and do not measure variation across training runs. The fixed magnetic-factor assignment also changes with flux (Appendix C). Establishing the ground-state field response requires checks of both initialization and this factor choice. The finite-cell comparison does not determine a thermodynamic phase boundary.

V Conclusion

Complex Psiformer combines complex hidden features and HMCVA with magnetic orbital sections for interacting continuum electrons. Both Psiformers lower the energies relative to their neural HF baselines. After the same number of optimization steps, Complex Psiformer reaches lower energies than Real Psiformer in both finite-supercell benchmarks. Its mean advantage in the 2525-cell system is 1.46​meV1.46\,\mathrm{meV} per electron over all five attempted training seeds. The separately trained N=2N=2 Complex state also has a smaller energy gap to the finite CI reference than its Real counterpart.

At the 1818-cell filling of 2/32/3 and nϕ=2n_{\phi}=2, the lower-energy Complex state has a clearer honeycomb-type density pattern, resembling the charge motif reported at different fields. The larger S⁡(K)S(K) relative to Real Psiformer mainly reflects the mean-density contribution. Across the independently optimized Complex states, density correlations vary nonmonotonically, with weaker honeycomb mean-density modulation at nϕ=4n_{\phi}=4 while connected fluctuations persist. These observations from a single finite cell do not establish crystal melting. The current maps provide a qualitative comparison of local phase-dependent circulation.

The energy gains apply to the complete architecture under the tested optimization settings. Component comparisons with matched tuning and computation budgets are needed to identify their origin. Energy decomposition and reference densities or currents would test the physical consequences of the improvement. Alternative magnetic sections and repeated optimizations would help assess the flux trends. Efficient derivative evaluation and transferable training may extend these tests to larger systems [26, 33, 15].
