Appendix A From Slater determinants to neural attention wavefunctions

A.1 Single-determinant reference and correlation energy

For NN spin-polarized electrons, we suppress the common spin factor. The Hartree–Fock (HF) reference is then a single determinant of orthonormal spatial orbitals that satisfy the prescribed magnetic boundary conditions:

ΨHF​(𝑹)=1N!​det[ϕj​(𝒓i)]i,j=1N.\Psi_{\mathrm{HF}}(\bm{R})=\frac{1}{\sqrt{N!}}\det\!\left[\phi_{j}(\bm{r}_{i})\right]_{i,j=1}^{N}. (24)

Here ii labels an electron row, and jj labels an orbital column. Exchanging two electron coordinates exchanges two rows and reverses the sign of the wavefunction. Each matrix element depends only on 𝒓i\bm{r}_{i}, so different electron coordinates couple only through antisymmetrization [43, 11]. This independent-orbital form restricts the accessible many-body sign and phase structure. For real states, it also restricts the nodal surface [12]. Let 𝒮1\mathcal{S}_{1} denote the nonzero single-determinant states in the same particle-number, spin-polarization, and magnetic-boundary sector. If E0E_{0} is the exact ground-state energy in this sector, the HF and correlation energies are

EHF=minΨ∈𝒮1⁡⟨Ψ|H^|Ψ⟩⟨Ψ|Ψ⟩,Ecorr=E0−EHF≤0.E_{\mathrm{HF}}=\min_{\Psi\in\mathcal{S}_{1}}\frac{\langle\Psi|\hat{H}|\Psi\rangle}{\langle\Psi|\Psi\rangle},\qquad E_{\mathrm{corr}}=E_{0}-E_{\mathrm{HF}}\leq 0. (25)

By the variational principle, the exact correlation energy is non-positive under the convention in Equation (25) [12, 16]. Energy differences between finite variational models should therefore not be identified with EcorrE_{\mathrm{corr}}. We compare variational energies directly for models optimized with the same Hamiltonian and boundary conditions. The D=1D=1 SlaterNet with configuration-independent orbitals has the single-determinant form of Equation (24). Its restricted neural parameterization and finite optimization need not attain EHFE_{\mathrm{HF}}. We therefore call the optimized Real and Complex D=1D=1 SlaterNets neural HF baselines. For each system, the energy reductions reported in Section IV.1 use the lower of the two neural HF estimates in Table 1 as a common reference. A multideterminant SlaterNet lies beyond 𝒮1\mathcal{S}_{1}. A Psiformer generally lies beyond the HF class even with one determinant, because its orbitals depend on the full electronic configuration.

A.2 Correlation mechanisms and neural extensions

Correlated fermionic ansatzes extend the independent-orbital determinant by introducing many-electron dependence into selected parts of the wavefunction. One representative form combines a Jastrow factor with a determinant expansion:

Ψ⁡(𝑹)=eJ⁡(𝑹)​∑k=1Kdet[ϕj(k)​(𝒒i​(𝑹))]i,j=1N.\Psi(\bm{R})=e^{J(\bm{R})}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\det\!\left[\phi_{j}^{(k)}\!\left(\bm{q}_{i}(\bm{R})\right)\right]_{i,j=1}^{N}.

Here J⁡(𝑹)J(\bm{R}) is exchange symmetric, and the backflow coordinate 𝒒i​(𝑹)\bm{q}_{i}(\bm{R}) is permutation equivariant. Fermionic antisymmetry therefore remains enforced by the determinants. For a real Jastrow factor, eJ⁡(𝑹)>0e^{J(\bm{R})}>0 changes the amplitude without altering the determinant zeros or phase [21, 12]. Its short-range form can also impose the Coulomb cusp condition [22]. A multideterminant expansion introduces interference between antisymmetric components. Backflow instead makes each orbital coordinate depend on the full configuration and can deform the determinant zero set [10, 24]. Continuous first-quantized neural wavefunctions use closely related mechanisms. PauliNet combines multireference orbitals with neural Jastrow and backflow factors. FermiNet constructs determinants from configuration-dependent orbitals [18, 39].

Neural backflow provides an analogous construction in lattice occupation space [29]. Correlation may therefore enter through symmetric many-body factors, determinant interference, or configuration-dependent orbital values. The SlaterNet–Psiformer hierarchy focuses on the last mechanism while retaining the same determinant-based antisymmetric readout. SlaterNet applies a shared neural map independently to each electron before the orbital readout [16]. Psiformer adds self-attention between electron streams, so each orbital coefficient can depend on the full configuration [47, 48]. The determinant expansion remains unchanged, so the architectures differ in how many-electron information reaches the orbital values before antisymmetrization.

Fu showed that a continuous fermionic wavefunction on a compact domain can be approximated by finite sums of antisymmetric basis functions with symmetric coefficients [14]. Here the basis functions and their symmetric coefficients are both continuous. The construction requires nontrivial antisymmetric basis functions that remain nonzero away from particle coincidences.

Table 2 compares the geometry, boundary conditions, and learned representation of related continuum wavefunctions. Complex Psiformer extends the periodic moiré setting of Ref. [16] to a magnetic torus and uses complex electron features and attention messages throughout the periodic coefficient network.

A.3 Periodic and magnetic neural wavefunctions

Periodic coordinate encoding, many-body correlation, and magnetic boundary conditions serve distinct roles in an extended-system neural wavefunction. For a supercell generated by 𝑳1\bm{L}_{1} and 𝑳2\bm{L}_{2}, the reciprocal vectors 𝑮a\bm{G}_{a} satisfy 𝑮a⋅𝑳b=2​π​δa​b\bm{G}_{a}\cdot\bm{L}_{b}=2\pi\delta_{ab}. Periodic coordinates can therefore be represented by Fourier features such as

𝒇0​(𝒓i)=(ei​𝑮1⋅𝒓i,ei​𝑮2⋅𝒓i).\bm{f}^{0}(\bm{r}_{i})=\left(e^{\mathrm{i}\bm{G}_{1}\cdot\bm{r}_{i}},e^{\mathrm{i}\bm{G}_{2}\cdot\bm{r}_{i}}\right).

The equivalent sine–cosine representation is widely used in neural wavefunctions for periodic solids [37, 5]. These features encode position on the finite torus without restricting the learned function to a finite plane-wave expansion. Generalized orbitals, backflow, message passing, pairing, and Bloch-based constructions can then add correlations to this periodic representation [27, 49, 38, 31, 30].

Within this hierarchy, SlaterNet and Psiformer differ in the periodic neural coefficient. SlaterNet retains a one-body form, whereas self-attention promotes the coefficient to a many-body representation. Shared attention maps make 𝒉iL​(𝑹)\bm{h}_{i}^{L}(\bm{R}) permutation equivariant. The coefficient associated with electron ii can therefore depend on all other coordinates before determinant antisymmetrization [48, 16]. Because the network uses periodic coordinate features, translating any electron by a supercell vector leaves the learned coefficient unchanged. This property holds for both real and complex hidden representations.

At nonzero magnetic flux, as shown in Figure 8, a uniform-field vector potential cannot be globally periodic on a torus carrying nonzero flux. Under a supercell translation, it instead returns to an equivalent gauge, 𝑨⁡(𝒓+𝑳a)=𝑨⁡(𝒓)+∇Λa​(𝒓)\bm{A}(\bm{r}+\bm{L}_{a})=\bm{A}(\bm{r})+\bm{\nabla}\Lambda_{a}(\bm{r}). Gauge covariance of the minimally coupled kinetic energy then requires a position-dependent wavefunction phase rather than ordinary periodicity [34, 17]. We impose this structure through fixed magnetic sections χj\chi_{j} satisfying χj​(𝒓i+𝑳a)=ei​Λa​(𝒓i)​χj​(𝒓i)\chi_{j}(\bm{r}_{i}+\bm{L}_{a})=e^{\mathrm{i}\Lambda_{a}(\bm{r}_{i})}\chi_{j}(\bm{r}_{i}). The learned coefficient carries the variational many-body dependence, while χj\chi_{j} supplies the prescribed magnetic transition law. At nϕ=0n_{\phi}=0, the section is omitted and the periodic neural coefficient directly supplies the orbital.

Previous neural wavefunctions have introduced magnetic structure through geometry-dependent envelopes, complex-valued factors, winding-aware readouts, or monopole harmonics [45, 36, 1, 40]. Winding-based constructions can also make the zeros of the magnetic orbital factor depend on the electronic configuration [1]. At finite field, our hierarchy keeps χj\chi_{j} fixed across all models and places the trainable many-electron dependence in the periodic coefficient. This coefficient may use real or complex features and may be attention free or configuration dependent. The model-specific attention rules and common MinSR settings are described below and in Appendix F.

A.4 Representations of neural network ansatzes

On a compact domain, a feed-forward neural network with a suitable nonlinear activation can approximate any continuous real-valued function arbitrarily well [20]. Applying this result separately to the real and imaginary parts gives a neural representation of continuous complex orbitals.

The models differ in the number field of the hidden electron representation and in whether electron streams communicate before the orbital readout. Real and Complex SlaterNets process electrons independently, whereas Real and Complex Psiformers communicate through attention. Within each architecture, the real and complex variants differ in their hidden parameterization. The final electron representation depends on the coordinates as

𝒉iL={𝒉L​(𝒓i),SlaterNets,𝒉iL​(𝑹),Psiformers.\bm{h}_{i}^{L}=\begin{cases}\bm{h}^{L}(\bm{r}_{i}),&\text{SlaterNets},\\[3.0pt] \bm{h}_{i}^{L}(\bm{R}),&\text{Psiformers}.\end{cases} (26)

The attention-free models therefore retain one-body orbitals even when several determinants are used. In Psiformer, attention makes the coefficient associated with electron ii depend on the full configuration. The determinant readout enforces fermionic antisymmetry in both cases. The real models use 𝒉iL∈ℝdL\bm{h}_{i}^{L}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\rm L}} and two real readouts to form a complex orbital coefficient. The complex models instead use 𝒉iL∈ℂdL\bm{h}_{i}^{L}\in\mathbb{C}^{d_{\rm L}} and one complex readout. With the same magnetic factor χj\chi_{j}, the orbital values are

ϕjm=χj​(𝒓i)​{𝒘j,Rm⋅𝒉iL+i​𝒘j,Im⋅𝒉iL,𝒉iL∈ℝdL,𝒘jm⋅𝒉iL,𝒉iL∈ℂdL.\phi_{j}^{m}=\chi_{j}(\bm{r}_{i})\begin{cases}\bm{w}_{j,\mathrm{R}}^{m}\cdot\bm{h}_{i}^{L}+\mathrm{i}\bm{w}_{j,\mathrm{I}}^{m}\cdot\bm{h}_{i}^{L},&\bm{h}_{i}^{L}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\rm L}},\\[4.0pt] \bm{w}_{j}^{m}\cdot\bm{h}_{i}^{L},&\bm{h}_{i}^{L}\in\mathbb{C}^{d_{\rm L}}.\end{cases}

The argument of 𝒉iL\bm{h}_{i}^{L} follows Equation (26). Both model classes can therefore produce complex orbital values. They differ in whether complex structure is retained within the hidden representation and, for Psiformer, within messages between electron streams [16]. One complex channel contains two real degrees of freedom. We therefore compare a complex width dLd_{\rm L} with a real width 2​dL2d_{\rm L}. This matching is consistent with the real-affine complex layers used here. For the map in Equation (7), with input and output widths dind_{\mathrm{in}} and doutd_{\mathrm{out}}, the number of real parameters is 4​dout​din+2​dout4d_{\mathrm{out}}d_{\mathrm{in}}+2d_{\mathrm{out}}. The map is equivalent to an unrestricted affine map from ℝ2​din\mathbb{R}^{2d_{\mathrm{in}}} to ℝ2​dout\mathbb{R}^{2d_{\mathrm{out}}}, with the same number of real parameters. The final term is absent for a bias-free map. The Psiformer comparison therefore matches the underlying hidden real dimensions without imposing equal total parameter counts. Appendix F reports the complete counts.

The radial activation and HMCVA can likewise be evaluated using paired real and imaginary components without changing the represented function. We checked an implementation using only real tensors throughout the network, magnetic factors, and determinant sum. In 24 synthetic cases with identical real parameter values, covering N=2,12N=2,12, nϕ=0,2n_{\phi}=0,2, and both branches of the residual limiter, the log-amplitude, unit phase, coordinate gradients, and gradients with respect to all real parameters agreed in double precision. The largest absolute difference in the parameter gradients was 2.74×10−122.74\times 10^{-12}. Full coordinate Hessians also agreed in four magnetic cases away from singular and switching points. These checks verify agreement at the tested configurations. The Real Psiformer baseline uses different nonlinearities and attention rules, as described below.

With the layer and HEAD indices suppressed, the attention message path in Real Psiformer is

αi​jR=softmaxj⁡[(𝒒iR)𝖳​𝒌jR],HEADiR=1dv​∑jαi​jR​𝒗jR.\alpha_{ij}^{\mathrm{R}}=\operatorname{softmax}_{j}\!\left[(\bm{q}_{i}^{\mathrm{R}})^{\mathsf{T}}\bm{k}_{j}^{\mathrm{R}}\right],\quad\operatorname{HEAD}_{i}^{\mathrm{R}}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{d_{v}}}\sum_{j}\alpha_{ij}^{\mathrm{R}}\bm{v}_{j}^{\mathrm{R}}.

Complex Psiformer instead uses

αi​jC=softmaxj⁡[|(𝒒iC)†​𝒌jC|dq],HEADiC=∑jαi​jC​𝒗jC.\alpha_{ij}^{\mathrm{C}}=\operatorname{softmax}_{j}\!\left[\frac{|(\bm{q}_{i}^{\mathrm{C}})^{\dagger}\bm{k}_{j}^{\mathrm{C}}|}{\sqrt{d_{q}}}\right],\quad\operatorname{HEAD}_{i}^{\mathrm{C}}=\sum_{j}\alpha_{ij}^{\mathrm{C}}\bm{v}_{j}^{\mathrm{C}}.

Both rules produce real, non-negative attention weights. Real Psiformer communicates real-valued features. HMCVA instead transports complex values through the value and residual streams. The Real Psiformer normalization follows Ref. [16]. It applies softmax to the unscaled real dot product and multiplies the aggregated value by dv−1/2d_{v}^{-1/2}. Scaling the score before softmax changes the relative attention weights. Scaling the aggregated value leaves those weights unchanged and changes the message amplitude. The HMCVA invariance discussed in Appendix D applies only to the scalar query–key compatibility. It does not imply gauge equivariance of the full network. At finite field, all models use the same nontrainable magnetic sections. The neural HF baselines use one determinant, while the Psiformers use four. The Psiformer pair matches the hidden real dimension, depth, and determinant count. The feature number field, activation, and attention rule remain model specific, and all models use MinSR. These settings define a comparison of the complete architectures.

Appendix B Periodic Coulomb interaction

The electrons are confined to two dimensions and interact through the Coulomb potential 1/r1/r. In a periodic supercell, we evaluate this interaction with an Ewald decomposition and a uniform neutralizing background [13, 12, 16].

Let Λ={n1𝑳1+n2𝑳2:n1,n2∈ℤ}\Lambda=\{n_{1}\bm{L}_{1}+n_{2}\bm{L}_{2}:n_{1},n_{2}\in\mathbb{Z}\} denote the supercell lattice and Λ∗={m1𝑮1+m2𝑮2:m1,m2∈ℤ}\Lambda^{\ast}=\{m_{1}\bm{G}_{1}+m_{2}\bm{G}_{2}:m_{1},m_{2}\in\mathbb{Z}\} its reciprocal lattice. The Ewald splitting length ηEw>0\eta_{\mathrm{Ew}}>0 separates the real- and reciprocal-space contributions. The resulting periodic pair interaction is

vEw​(𝒓)=\displaystyle v_{\mathrm{Ew}}(\bm{r})={} ∑𝑳∈Λerfc⁡(|𝒓+𝑳|/(2​ηEw))|𝒓+𝑳|\displaystyle\sum_{\bm{L}\in\Lambda}\frac{\operatorname{erfc}\!\left(|\bm{r}+\bm{L}|/(2\eta_{\mathrm{Ew}})\right)}{|\bm{r}+\bm{L}|}
+2​πΩ∑𝑮∈Λ∗𝑮≠𝟎erfc⁡(ηEw​|𝑮|)|𝑮|cos(𝑮⋅𝒓)−4​π​ηEwΩ.\displaystyle+\frac{2\pi}{\Omega}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\bm{G}\in\Lambda^{\ast}\\ \bm{G}\neq\bm{0}\end{subarray}}\frac{\operatorname{erfc}(\eta_{\mathrm{Ew}}|\bm{G}|)}{|\bm{G}|}\cos(\bm{G}\cdot\bm{r})-\frac{4\sqrt{\pi}\eta_{\mathrm{Ew}}}{\Omega}.

The neutralizing background removes the reciprocal zero mode and produces the final constant term.

The regular part of the periodic interaction at the origin defines the corresponding Madelung constant,

ξM=lim𝒓→𝟎[vEw​(𝒓)−1|𝒓|].\xi_{\mathrm{M}}={}\lim_{\bm{r}\to\bm{0}}\left[v_{\mathrm{Ew}}(\bm{r})-\frac{1}{|\bm{r}|}\right].

The complete periodic Coulomb contribution to Equation (3) is

Vee​(𝑹)=∑i<jvEw​(𝒓i−𝒓j)+N2​ξM.V_{\mathrm{ee}}(\bm{R})=\sum_{i<j}v_{\mathrm{Ew}}(\bm{r}_{i}-\bm{r}_{j})+\frac{N}{2}\xi_{\mathrm{M}}.

We checked the Ewald truncation on 256 fixed N=12N=12 configurations from a scrambled Sobol sequence for each supercell. Increasing both index cutoffs from 5 to 16 gave maximum changes in Vee/NV_{\mathrm{ee}}/N of 2.07×10−42.07\times 10^{-4} and 2.10×10−8​meV2.10\times 10^{-8}\,\mathrm{meV} in the 1818- and 2525-cell geometries, respectively. The cutoff-12 results agreed with the reference to double-precision roundoff, as did a 25% variation of the splitting length at cutoff 16. These maxima apply to the fixed configuration set used for this truncation check.

Appendix C Construction of the magnetic sections

The neural orbital coefficients introduced in the main text are periodic under supercell translations. At nonzero magnetic flux, the complete orbital must also acquire the position-dependent phase in Equation (4). We impose this boundary law through fixed functions χj\chi_{j}. This appendix constructs them for the oblique supercells used in our calculations, following the torus Landau-level representation of Ref. [34].

Let 𝑳1\bm{L}_{1} and 𝑳2\bm{L}_{2} denote the oriented supercell translation vectors, with area Ω=|𝑳1×𝑳2|>0\Omega=|\bm{L}_{1}\times\bm{L}_{2}|>0. The uniform magnetic field is perpendicular to the plane, 𝑩=B​𝒛^\bm{B}=B\hat{\bm{z}}. In the charge-weighted convention of the Hamiltonian, B>0B>0 is the field strength and satisfies B​Ω=2​π​nϕB\Omega=2\pi n_{\phi}. Here nϕ∈ℕ>0n_{\phi}\in\mathbb{N}_{>0} is the number of flux quanta through the supercell. We center the symmetric gauge at 𝒍=(𝑳1+𝑳2)/2\bm{l}=(\bm{L}_{1}+\bm{L}_{2})/2.

We resolve the oblique cell into directions parallel and perpendicular to 𝑳1\bm{L}_{1}. The associated length and unit vectors are

L∥=|𝑳1|,𝒆∥=𝑳1L∥,𝒆⟂=𝒛^×𝒆∥.L_{\parallel}=|\bm{L}_{1}|,\qquad\bm{e}_{\parallel}=\frac{\bm{L}_{1}}{L_{\parallel}},\qquad\bm{e}_{\perp}=\hat{\bm{z}}\times\bm{e}_{\parallel}.

The shear ss and perpendicular cell length L⟂L_{\perp} are

s=𝑳2⋅𝒆∥,L⟂=𝑳2⋅𝒆⟂>0.s=\bm{L}_{2}\cdot\bm{e}_{\parallel},\qquad L_{\perp}=\bm{L}_{2}\cdot\bm{e}_{\perp}>0.

These definitions give 𝑳1=L∥​𝒆∥\bm{L}_{1}=L_{\parallel}\bm{e}_{\parallel}, 𝑳2=s​𝒆∥+L⟂​𝒆⟂\bm{L}_{2}=s\bm{e}_{\parallel}+L_{\perp}\bm{e}_{\perp}, and Ω=L∥​L⟂\Omega=L_{\parallel}L_{\perp}.

For the NN-electron determinant, we assign two nonnegative integer labels to each orbital column j=1,…,Nj=1,\ldots,N:

μj=(j−1)modnϕ,νj=⌊j−1nϕ⌋.\mu_{j}=(j-1)\bmod n_{\phi},\qquad\nu_{j}=\left\lfloor\frac{j-1}{n_{\phi}}\right\rfloor.

The label μj∈{0,…,nϕ−1}\mu_{j}\in\{0,\ldots,n_{\phi}-1\} selects a magnetic-translation sector, while νj\nu_{j} selects a transverse oscillator channel. For each integer image index n∈ℤn\in\mathbb{Z}, the longitudinal wave number is

kj​n=2​π​μjL∥+B​L⟂​n.k_{jn}=\frac{2\pi\mu_{j}}{L_{\parallel}}+BL_{\perp}n.

Here kj​0=2​π​μj/L∥k_{j0}=2\pi\mu_{j}/L_{\parallel} denotes the n=0n=0 member of this sequence.

All models use the same column assignment at a given flux. Changing nϕn_{\phi} in the flux scan also changes the assigned oscillator channels. At zero flux the magnetic factors are omitted. The scan does not assess sensitivity to alternative assignments.

In a uniform field, the corresponding Landau-gauge functions separate into a plane wave along 𝒆∥\bm{e}_{\parallel} and a harmonic-oscillator profile along 𝒆⟂\bm{e}_{\perp} [34]. The channel νj\nu_{j} selects the normalized transverse profile

φν​(ξ)=Hν(ξ)e−ξ2/2(2ν​ν!​π)1/2,ξ∈ℝ,\varphi_{\nu}(\xi)=\frac{H_{\nu}(\xi)e^{-\xi^{2}/2}}{\left(2^{\nu}\nu!\sqrt{\pi}\right)^{1/2}},\qquad\xi\in\mathbb{R},

where HνH_{\nu} is the physicists’ Hermite polynomial of order ν=0,1,…\nu=0,1,\ldots.

Let 𝒓¯\overline{\bm{r}} denote the representative of 𝒓\bm{r} in the canonical supercell centered at 𝒍\bm{l}. Its scalar coordinates relative to the gauge center are

x∥=(𝒓¯−𝒍)⋅𝒆∥,x⟂=(𝒓¯−𝒍)⋅𝒆⟂.x_{\parallel}=(\overline{\bm{r}}-\bm{l})\cdot\bm{e}_{\parallel},\qquad x_{\perp}=(\overline{\bm{r}}-\bm{l})\cdot\bm{e}_{\perp}.

Within this canonical cell, the jjth magnetic section is

χ~j​(𝒓¯)=B1/4L∥​exp⁡(i​B​x∥​x⟂2)×∑n∈ℤφνj​[B​(x⟂+kj​nB)]×exp⁡(i​x∥​kj​n)​exp⁡[i⁡(n​kj​0​s+12​B​L⟂​s​n2)].\begin{multlined}\widetilde{\chi}_{j}(\overline{\bm{r}})=\frac{B^{1/4}}{\sqrt{L_{\parallel}}}\exp\!\left(\frac{\mathrm{i}Bx_{\parallel}x_{\perp}}{2}\right)\\ {}\times\sum_{n\in\mathbb{Z}}\varphi_{\nu_{j}}\!\left[\sqrt{B}\left(x_{\perp}+\frac{k_{jn}}{B}\right)\right]\\ {}\times\exp(\mathrm{i}x_{\parallel}k_{jn})\exp\!\left[\mathrm{i}\left(nk_{j0}s+\frac{1}{2}BL_{\perp}sn^{2}\right)\right].\end{multlined} (27)

The Hermite function and exp⁡(i​x∥​kj​n)\exp(\mathrm{i}x_{\parallel}k_{jn}) form the Landau-gauge orbital. The final exponential accounts for the shear of the oblique cell. The factor containing x∥​x⟂x_{\parallel}x_{\perp} converts the orbital to the cell-centered symmetric gauge used in the Hamiltonian.

The boundary phases follow directly from this infinite sum. Under translation by 𝑳1\bm{L}_{1}, the identity kj​n​L∥=2​π​(μj+nϕ​n)k_{jn}L_{\parallel}=2\pi(\mu_{j}+n_{\phi}n) leaves each plane-wave factor unchanged, and the prefactor supplies ei​B​L∥​x⟂/2e^{\mathrm{i}BL_{\parallel}x_{\perp}/2}. Translation by 𝑳2\bm{L}_{2} sends (x∥,x⟂)(x_{\parallel},x_{\perp}) to (x∥+s,x⟂+L⟂)(x_{\parallel}+s,x_{\perp}+L_{\perp}). Using kj,n+1=kj​n+B​L⟂k_{j,n+1}=k_{jn}+BL_{\perp} to shift the image index restores the oscillator argument. Combining the remaining phases gives ei​B​(s​x⟂−L⟂​x∥)/2e^{\mathrm{i}B(sx_{\perp}-L_{\perp}x_{\parallel})/2}. These are the factors ei​Λa​(𝒓¯)e^{\mathrm{i}\Lambda_{a}(\overline{\bm{r}})} in Equation (4). Differentiating the identities gives the corresponding matching of covariant derivatives.

In the numerical implementation, we truncate the image sum to |n|≤8|n|\leq 8, as listed in Table 5. At finite cutoff, shifting the image index leaves endpoint terms. The winding construction below enforces whole-cell translation phases, while matching across the cell seams depends on the truncated tails.

Increasing the cutoff to 12 and 16 gave agreement to double-precision roundoff for the fixed functions and their first and second coordinate derivatives. We tested both supercell geometries with N=12N=12 and nϕ=1,…,4n_{\phi}=1,\ldots,4, together with the N=2N=2, nϕ=2n_{\phi}=2 benchmark. Each case used 384 points, including 128 near the cell seams. We also evaluated the finite sum at 16 points on each boundary. After applying the boundary phase, the values, covariant gradients, and covariant Laplacians matched to double-precision roundoff. These checks concern the fixed magnetic functions and do not bound errors in the full neural wavefunction.

To extend the section beyond the canonical cell, write an arbitrary position as 𝒓=𝒓¯+w1​𝑳1+w2​𝑳2\bm{r}=\overline{\bm{r}}+w_{1}\bm{L}_{1}+w_{2}\bm{L}_{2}, where w1,w2∈ℤw_{1},w_{2}\in\mathbb{Z} count windings along the two supercell directions. For a=1,2a=1,2, the symmetric-gauge transition function is

Λa​(𝒓)=B2​[𝑳a×(𝒓−𝒍)]z.\Lambda_{a}(\bm{r})=\frac{B}{2}\left[\bm{L}_{a}\times(\bm{r}-\bm{l})\right]_{z}.

A path that first winds along 𝑳1\bm{L}_{1} and then along 𝑳2\bm{L}_{2} gives

χj​(𝒓)=exp⁡[i​w1​Λ1​(𝒓¯)+i​w2​Λ2​(𝒓¯+w1​𝑳1)]​χ~j​(𝒓¯).\chi_{j}(\bm{r})=\exp\!\left[\mathrm{i}w_{1}\Lambda_{1}(\overline{\bm{r}})+\mathrm{i}w_{2}\Lambda_{2}(\overline{\bm{r}}+w_{1}\bm{L}_{1})\right]\widetilde{\chi}_{j}(\overline{\bm{r}}).

The two possible winding orders differ by

ei​Λ2​(𝒓+𝑳1)​ei​Λ1​(𝒓)ei​Λ1​(𝒓+𝑳2)​ei​Λ2​(𝒓)=e−i​B​Ω=1.\frac{e^{\mathrm{i}\Lambda_{2}(\bm{r}+\bm{L}_{1})}e^{\mathrm{i}\Lambda_{1}(\bm{r})}}{e^{\mathrm{i}\Lambda_{1}(\bm{r}+\bm{L}_{2})}e^{\mathrm{i}\Lambda_{2}(\bm{r})}}=e^{-\mathrm{i}B\Omega}=1.

Flux quantization makes the extension independent of the winding order and yields the required transition law

χj(𝒓+𝑳a)=ei​Λa​(𝒓)χj(𝒓),a=1,2.\chi_{j}(\bm{r}+\bm{L}_{a})=e^{\mathrm{i}\Lambda_{a}(\bm{r})}\chi_{j}(\bm{r}),\qquad a=1,2. (28)

The functions χj\chi_{j} remain fixed during optimization and are shared by all four neural models. They supply the magnetic boundary law, while the learned orbital coefficients retain the variational dependence on electron coordinates. Translating electron ii by 𝑳a\bm{L}_{a} multiplies every element in determinant row ii by the same factor ei​Λa​(𝒓i)e^{\mathrm{i}\Lambda_{a}(\bm{r}_{i})}. The determinant therefore satisfies the many-body magnetic boundary condition [17]. Although the construction uses Landau-level functions, the unrestricted periodic neural coefficient does not project the variational orbital onto a fixed Landau-level subspace.

For the frozen 2525-cell, N=12N=12, nϕ=2n_{\phi}=2 seed-11 Psiformers, we checked both primitive seams using two background configurations, moving each electron in turn. The wavefunction and its covariant directional derivatives were compared on opposite sides at fractional displacements from 10−210^{-2} to 10−810^{-8} along the corresponding primitive vector. At the smallest displacement, the largest value difference divided by the larger wavefunction amplitude in each pair was 3.13×10−63.13\times 10^{-6}. For both models, the maximum value mismatch decreased as the displacement was reduced. These finite probes assess local matching at the tested configurations.

Appendix D Structural properties of Complex Psiformer

Multiplying either the query or the key by a unit complex phase leaves the Hermitian-magnitude score in Equation (13) unchanged. The overlap phase therefore does not enter the real attention weight. Changes in the query or key magnitudes do change the score. Phase information remains in the complex values and hidden representations. This score invariance does not imply gauge equivariance of the full network, whose projections are general real-linear maps.

We first verify exchange symmetry. Let Π\Pi be an N×NN\times N permutation matrix that reorders the electron coordinates in 𝑹=(𝒓1,…,𝒓N)\bm{R}=(\bm{r}_{1},\ldots,\bm{r}_{N}) and the corresponding rows of each hidden array. Write 𝑯l∈ℂN×dL\bm{H}^{l}\in\mathbb{C}^{N\times d_{\rm L}} for the array with iith row 𝒉il\bm{h}_{i}^{l}. The query, key, and value maps are shared across electron rows. Permuting the input therefore permutes their row labels. The score in Equation (13) carries one receiver and one source label, so the same permutation relabels both indices. Row-wise softmax and the sum in Equation (14) commute with this relabeling. The output projection and residual perceptron are also shared across rows. Consequently,

𝑯L​(Π​𝑹)=Π​𝑯L​(𝑹).\bm{H}^{L}(\Pi\bm{R})=\Pi\bm{H}^{L}(\bm{R}).

The fixed functions χj​(𝒓i)\chi_{j}(\bm{r}_{i}) are evaluated row by row and transform in the same way. An electron permutation therefore only reorders the rows of each orbital array [ϕjm​(𝒓i,{𝒓/i})]i,j=1N[\phi_{j}^{m}(\bm{r}_{i};\{\bm{r}_{/i}\})]_{i,j=1}^{N}. Every determinant acquires the same factor det(Π)\det(\Pi), and

Ψ⁡(Π​𝑹)=det(Π)​Ψ​(𝑹).\Psi(\Pi\bm{R})=\det(\Pi)\Psi(\bm{R}).

For an exchange of two electrons, det(Π)=−1\det(\Pi)=-1. The wavefunction is therefore fermionically antisymmetric.

The magnetic boundary condition follows independently. Translating electron ii by 𝑳a\bm{L}_{a} leaves its learned periodic coefficient unchanged. The section χj\chi_{j} multiplies every entry in row ii by the common transition factor in Equation (28). Because the determinant is linear in that row,

Ψ⁡(…,𝒓i+𝑳a,…)=ei​Λa​(𝒓i)​Ψ​(…,𝒓i,…).\Psi(\ldots,\bm{r}_{i}+\bm{L}_{a},\ldots)=e^{\mathrm{i}\Lambda_{a}(\bm{r}_{i})}\Psi(\ldots,\bm{r}_{i},\ldots).

This reproduces the many-body magnetic boundary condition in Equation (4).

Appendix E Complex VMC optimization

During training, Metropolis–Hastings sampling uses ratios of |Ψ|2|\Psi|^{2}, so the wavefunction normalization is not needed. For a symmetric proposal, the log probability ratio is 2​[u𝜽​(𝑹′)−u𝜽​(𝑹)]2[u_{\bm{\theta}}(\bm{R}^{\prime})-u_{\bm{\theta}}(\bm{R})]. Evaluating this ratio in log amplitude avoids numerical overflow and underflow. We derive the magnetic local energy and MinSR update below, and describe the independent energy evaluation separately.

E.1 Magnetic local energy

In a magnetic field, the kinetic energy depends on both the amplitude and spatial phase of a complex wavefunction. Locally away from nodes, write

Ψ⁡(𝑹)=eu⁡(𝑹)​ei​ϕ​(𝑹),u⁡(𝑹)=log⁡|Ψ⁡(𝑹)|.\Psi(\bm{R})=e^{u(\bm{R})}e^{\mathrm{i}\phi(\bm{R})},\quad u(\bm{R})=\log|\Psi(\bm{R})|.

For the kinetic operator in Equation (3),

T^=12​∑i(−i​∇i−𝑨i)2,𝑨i=𝑨⁡(𝒓i),\hat{T}=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{i}\left(-\mathrm{i}\bm{\nabla}_{i}-\bm{A}_{i}\right)^{2},\quad\bm{A}_{i}=\bm{A}(\bm{r}_{i}),

where ∇i⋅𝑨i=0\bm{\nabla}_{i}\cdot\bm{A}_{i}=0 in the symmetric gauge. The kinetic local energy is

Tloc​(𝑹)=\displaystyle T_{\mathrm{loc}}(\bm{R})= −12∑i[∇i2u+|∇iu|2−|∇iϕ−𝑨i|2\displaystyle-\frac{1}{2}\sum_{i}\Big[\nabla_{i}^{2}u+|\bm{\nabla}_{i}u|^{2}-|\bm{\nabla}_{i}\phi-\bm{A}_{i}|^{2} (29)
+i(∇i2ϕ+2∇iu⋅(∇iϕ−𝑨i))].\displaystyle+\mathrm{i}\big(\nabla_{i}^{2}\phi+2\bm{\nabla}_{i}u\cdot(\bm{\nabla}_{i}\phi-\bm{A}_{i})\big)\Big].

The phase gradient and vector potential enter together through ∇iϕ−𝑨i\bm{\nabla}_{i}\phi-\bm{A}_{i}. The Monte Carlo distribution depends only on |Ψ|2=e2​u|\Psi|^{2}=e^{2u}, while the magnetic kinetic energy depends explicitly on the phase through ∇iϕ−𝑨i\bm{\nabla}_{i}\phi-\bm{A}_{i}. Adding the moiré potential and Coulomb interaction gives the full local energy,

Eloc​(𝑹)=\displaystyle E_{\mathrm{loc}}(\bm{R})= Tloc​(𝑹)+∑iVM​(𝒓i)\displaystyle T_{\mathrm{loc}}(\bm{R})+\sum_{i}V_{\mathrm{M}}(\bm{r}_{i}) (30)
+∑i<jvEw(𝒓i−𝒓j)+N2ξM.\displaystyle+\sum_{i<j}v_{\mathrm{Ew}}(\bm{r}_{i}-\bm{r}_{j})+\frac{N}{2}\xi_{\mathrm{M}}.

The local energy at configuration 𝑹\bm{R} is a pointwise ratio, not a configuration-dependent eigenvalue. For an approximate complex trial state, [H^​Ψ]​(𝑹)[\hat{H}\Psi](\bm{R}) need not share the phase of Ψ⁡(𝑹)\Psi(\bm{R}). Consequently, Eloc​(𝑹)E_{\mathrm{loc}}(\bm{R}) may be complex, while its probability-weighted average is the real Rayleigh quotient in Equation (16) when the trial state belongs to the operator domain of the self-adjoint Hamiltonian with the prescribed magnetic boundary condition. Under this condition, the imaginary part cancels in the exact expectation, although a finite Monte Carlo batch may retain a statistical imaginary residual. For an exact eigenstate, the local energy equals the same real eigenvalue at every non-nodal configuration [12]. The configuration-dependent imaginary part must still be retained because it couples to the phase response in the energy gradient.

E.2 Independent energy evaluation

We evaluate the trained Psiformer states in Section IV.1 with the magnetic quadratic form,

E=⟨12​∑i[|∇iu|2+|∇iϕ−𝑨i|2]+V⁡(𝑹)⟩|Ψ|2,E=\left\langle\frac{1}{2}\sum_{i}\left[|\bm{\nabla}_{i}u|^{2}+|\bm{\nabla}_{i}\phi-\bm{A}_{i}|^{2}\right]+V(\bm{R})\right\rangle_{|\Psi|^{2}},

where VV contains the moiré potential and the complete periodic Coulomb interaction. For a normalized trial state satisfying the magnetic boundary condition, square-integrable first covariant derivatives in the weak sense and a finite potential-energy integral suffice to define this variational energy. A classical Laplacian at every configuration is not required. For states in the operator domain, integration by parts recovers the local-energy expectation. For nonsmooth trial states, derivative jumps can contribute interface terms that a pointwise Laplacian omits. Statistical convergence of the estimates must be assessed separately.

With the denominator regularization described after Equation (8), the implemented activation is continuously differentiable in the real and imaginary parts of its input, including at zero. Its second derivatives are generally not continuous there. The regularity of the full ansatz also depends on the absolute-value attention score, residual rescaling, and magnetic boundary matching.

The conventional Complex-Psiformer local-energy samples have heavy tails and show finite-sample differences from the quadratic-form estimates. We use the same quadratic-form protocol for the independent Real–Complex Psiformer comparisons. The conventional complex local energy remains the training signal and an evaluation diagnostic.

Table 1 retains the conventional local-energy summaries after 10,000 training steps. The HF entries use Real-SlaterNet seed 11 and Complex-SlaterNet seed 00. For the 1818-cell entries, the quoted uncertainties are the local-energy sample standard deviations divided by 384\sqrt{384}. They neglect correlations between samples and describe neither variation across training seeds nor uncertainty in the converged HF minimum. The HF-relative energy reductions use these conventional estimates throughout. The independent quadratic-form evaluations provide the quantitative Real–Complex Psiformer comparison.

Training uses configurations sampled from |Ψ𝜽|2|\Psi_{\bm{\theta}}|^{2}. After fixing the trained parameters, we evaluate the state using a sampling density proportional to |Ψ|2​α|\Psi|^{2\alpha}. The exponent 0<α<10<\alpha<1 increases the relative probability of visiting low-amplitude regions, where kinetic-energy estimators can fluctuate strongly. Ordinary sampling is recovered at α=1\alpha=1. For an observable OO, we estimate its expectation under |Ψ|2|\Psi|^{2} by ∑sws​O​(𝑹s)/∑sws\sum_{s}w_{s}O(\bm{R}_{s})/\sum_{s}w_{s}, with ws=|Ψ⁡(𝑹s)|2​(1−α)w_{s}=|\Psi(\bm{R}_{s})|^{2(1-\alpha)} for sampled configurations 𝑹s\bm{R}_{s}. This reweighting leaves the target expectation unchanged in the sampling limit. The exponent controls evaluation only and does not alter the trained wavefunction.

The primary evaluation uses α=0.900\alpha=0.900, 384 walkers, 20,000 burn-in transitions, and 1,024 retained sweeps separated by 20 Metropolis transitions, giving 393,216 retained configurations per state. The network parameters, proposal scale, and estimator settings remain fixed, and all retained configurations enter the estimates without clipping. An independent calculation with α=0.750\alpha=0.750 checks sensitivity to broader sampling for the N=2N=2 and 2525-cell benchmarks.

Sampling standard errors are estimated from 16 consecutive time blocks for the 1818-cell, N=12N=12 states and 12 fixed walker groups for N=2N=2 and the 2525-cell, N=12N=12 states. Each time block contains 64 retained sweeps of all walkers, while each walker group contains 32 trajectories over all retained sweeps. We recompute the self-normalized estimate within each block or group. The sampling standard error is the sample standard deviation of these estimates divided by the square root of their number. For the 1818-cell seed-11 pair at nϕ=2n_{\phi}=2, the Complex and Real energies are −57.4-57.4 and −55.5​meV-55.5\,\mathrm{meV} per electron, with standard errors of 0.1360.136 and 0.0727​meV0.0727\,\mathrm{meV} per electron. The corresponding N=2N=2 energies are −29.0-29.0 and −12.1​meV-12.1\,\mathrm{meV} per electron, with standard errors of 0.06570.0657 and 0.165​meV0.165\,\mathrm{meV} per electron. Adding the squared sampling standard errors and taking the square root gives standard errors of 0.1540.154 and 0.178​meV0.178\,\mathrm{meV} per electron for the respective energy differences. These empirical errors describe sampling at fixed parameters. In the 2525-cell comparison, the descriptive standard error of the difference between the two five-seed means is 0.484​meV0.484\,\mathrm{meV} per electron, obtained by adding the two sample variances divided by five and taking the square root, with no covariance assigned between models. Matching seed indices does not imply paired initial wavefunctions or sampling trajectories. The observed spread of endpoint estimates also contains residual Monte Carlo noise. Individual primary energies and their sampling errors are supplied in data/25cell_seed_energies.csv.

For the 1818-cell, N=12N=12 Complex and Real states, the importance-weight effective sample sizes are 0.8040.804 and 0.7820.782 of the retained counts. These fractions measure weight concentration and omit Markov-chain autocorrelation. The first and second halves of the evaluations, summarized by the means of their block estimates, differ by 0.1890.189 and 0.150​meV0.150\,\mathrm{meV} per electron. Doubling the block length to 128 retained sweeps gives standard errors of 0.1400.140 and 0.0928​meV0.0928\,\mathrm{meV} per electron for Complex and Real, respectively. Additional block lengths from 1 to 256 sweeps are reported in the accompanying data.

We also assess how strongly individual configurations affect these energy estimates. On omitting one configuration at a time, the largest observed changes are 0.1140.114 and 0.00491​meV0.00491\,\mathrm{meV} per electron for Complex and Real, respectively. These omissions serve only as sensitivity checks, and all configurations remain in the reported estimates. The energy ordering of this frozen pair survives these checks, while the errors remain sensitive to blocking and rare sampled configurations. Longer independent evaluations are needed to assess residual sampling bias and contributions from unvisited regions with large spatial derivatives.

Figure 9 separates the N=2N=2 energy comparison from its sampling check. The Complex and Real states lie 5.715.71 and 22.6​meV22.6\,\mathrm{meV} per electron above the 40-orbital, 780-determinant CI reference. Changing the evaluation exponent from 0.9000.900 to 0.7500.750 shifts their energies by −0.00899-0.00899 and 0.450​meV0.450\,\mathrm{meV} per electron, respectively. The Complex shift is small relative to its combined sampling error of 0.107​meV0.107\,\mathrm{meV} per electron. The Real shift is about 2.112.11 times its combined error of 0.213​meV0.213\,\mathrm{meV} per electron, indicating residual sampling sensitivity. Both evaluations retain the same energy ordering for this single training pair. The plotted gaps use the fixed CI matrix energy as the reference. Their error bars describe neural-state sampling and exclude the residual error of the finite CI basis.

E.3 Finite CI reference

To construct the N=2N=2 reference, we orthonormalize 448 torus Landau functions spanning 224 Landau levels on a 96×12896\times 128 midpoint grid. We diagonalize the one-body Hamiltonian, including the moiré potential, in this basis and retain its 40 lowest eigenstates. All 780 two-electron determinants formed from these orbitals enter the CI calculation. Coulomb matrix elements are assembled from Fourier transforms of orbital products, using supercell reciprocal indices from −16-16 to 1616 and omitting the zero vector. The Madelung self term is included once. The magnetic image cutoff is 12, and the Ewald self term uses cutoff 8.

With the other cutoffs fixed, increasing the Landau-level count from 192 to 224 changes the energy by 8.93×10−4​meV8.93\times 10^{-4}\,\mathrm{meV} per electron. Enlarging the active space from 36 to 40 orbitals changes it by 3.90×10−5​meV3.90\times 10^{-5}\,\mathrm{meV} per electron. These finite-cutoff changes do not bound the remaining error relative to the continuum ground state.

An independent coordinate-space check of the same frozen CI state uses 16 scrambled Sobol replicates, each with 2172^{17} configurations. The energy evaluated with the production Ewald interaction minus the CI matrix energy is (−2.30±2.09)×10−4​meV(-2.30\pm 2.09)\times 10^{-4}\,\mathrm{meV} per electron. The estimate uses the ratio of the pooled energy and normalization integrals. Its empirical standard error is obtained across the randomized replicates, retaining the covariance between numerator and denominator.

E.4 Sample-space MinSR

Wavefunction optimization must retain the phase dependence of the magnetic local energy. For a batch {𝑹b}b=1M\{\bm{R}_{b}\}_{b=1}^{M}, define the centered local energy

E~b=Eloc,𝜽​(𝑹b)−1M​∑b′=1MEloc,𝜽​(𝑹b′).\widetilde{E}_{b}=E_{\mathrm{loc},\bm{\theta}}(\bm{R}_{b})-\frac{1}{M}\sum_{b^{\prime}=1}^{M}E_{\mathrm{loc},\bm{\theta}}(\bm{R}_{b^{\prime}}).

Using the amplitude and phase derivatives Jb​μu=∂θμu𝜽​(𝑹b)J^{u}_{b\mu}=\partial_{\theta_{\mu}}u_{\bm{\theta}}(\bm{R}_{b}) and Jb​μϕ=∂θμϕ𝜽​(𝑹b)J^{\phi}_{b\mu}=\partial_{\theta_{\mu}}\phi_{\bm{\theta}}(\bm{R}_{b}), we obtain the Monte Carlo energy-gradient estimator under the assumptions stated in Section III.2,

gμ=2M​∑b[J~b​μu​Re⁡E~b+J~b​μϕ​Im⁡E~b],g_{\mu}=\frac{2}{M}\sum_{b}\left[\widetilde{J}^{u}_{b\mu}\operatorname{Re}\widetilde{E}_{b}+\widetilde{J}^{\phi}_{b\mu}\operatorname{Im}\widetilde{E}_{b}\right],

Here the tilde denotes subtraction of the batch mean. The amplitude response couples to the real part of the local-energy fluctuation, while the phase response couples to its imaginary part. Both terms contribute to the variational energy gradient.

Stochastic reconfiguration measures updates through their effect on the wavefunction. Retaining both amplitude and phase responses gives the real SR metric [44],

Sμ​ν=1M​∑b(J~b​μu​J~b​νu+J~b​μϕ​J~b​νϕ).S_{\mu\nu}=\frac{1}{M}\sum_{b}\left(\widetilde{J}^{u}_{b\mu}\widetilde{J}^{u}_{b\nu}+\widetilde{J}^{\phi}_{b\mu}\widetilde{J}^{\phi}_{b\nu}\right). (31)

Stacking the centered Jacobians into the matrix XX defined in Equation (18), we introduce

𝒚=1M​(Re⁡𝑬~Im⁡𝑬~),𝑬~=(E~1E~M).\bm{y}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{M}}\begin{pmatrix}\operatorname{Re}\widetilde{\bm{E}}\\ \operatorname{Im}\widetilde{\bm{E}}\end{pmatrix},\qquad\widetilde{\bm{E}}=\begin{pmatrix}\widetilde{E}_{1}\\ \vdots\\ \widetilde{E}_{M}\end{pmatrix}.

The metric and gradient then become

S=X𝖳​X,𝒈=2​X𝖳​𝒚.S=X^{\mathsf{T}}X,\qquad\bm{g}=2X^{\mathsf{T}}\bm{y}.

A direct SR update requires a linear solve in the PP-dimensional parameter space. The push-through identity evaluates the same update in sample space,

Δ​𝜽\displaystyle\Delta\bm{\theta} =−η​(S+λ​IP)−1​𝒈\displaystyle=-\eta\left(S+\lambda I_{P}\right)^{-1}\bm{g} (32)
=−2​η​X𝖳​(X​X𝖳+λ​I2​M)−1​𝒚.\displaystyle=-2\eta X^{\mathsf{T}}\left(XX^{\mathsf{T}}+\lambda I_{2M}\right)^{-1}\bm{y}.

This is the sample-space form used in MinSR [6, 42]. It reduces the linear solve from the PP-dimensional parameter space to the 2​M2M-dimensional sample space. The parameters and linear system remain real. The complex wavefunction enters through the amplitude and phase responses JuJ^{u} and JϕJ^{\phi}, together with the real and imaginary parts of the centered local energy.

The push-through identity in Equation (32) is an algebraically exact rewrite of the damped SR update for the sampled metric. It retains correlations among all real trainable parameters within the finite batch, without factorizing the metric by layer. The 2​M2M-dimensional MinSR system includes both amplitude and phase responses. All models in the main comparison use the same implementation and numerical settings.

In training, the real and imaginary local energies are clipped separately to three median absolute deviations about their respective batch medians. The clipped components are then centered to construct 𝒚\bm{y}. After the MinSR solve, we rescale the update by a common factor if its squared norm in the sampled SR metric exceeds the constraint listed in Tables 3 and 4. Clipping changes the energy-gradient estimator and is confined to the optimization target. The independent quadratic-form evaluations retain all sampled values without clipping.

E.5 Auxiliary KFAC comparison

KFAC approximates the parameter-space metric with layer-wise Kronecker factors [32]. This reduces the cost of storing and inverting the full metric but neglects correlations between different layer blocks. Ref. [16] also used KFAC to optimize Real Psiformer. We therefore compare KFAC and MinSR for the same Real Psiformer model at nϕ=0,1,n_{\phi}=0,1, and 22, as shown in Figure 10.

MinSR reaches a lower variational energy at nϕ=0n_{\phi}=0, even without magnetic flux. The difference increases substantially at finite flux. At both nϕ=1n_{\phi}=1 and 22, the KFAC trajectories saturate at higher energies, while MinSR continues to lower the energy. This comparison motivates the use of MinSR in the main benchmark.

Appendix F Network and optimization hyperparameters

Calculations and derived comparisons use the unrounded values. Tables 3, 4, and 5 list the frozen settings for the main four-model benchmark. The neural HF baselines use one determinant, while the Psiformers use four. All models have three neural layers and share the sampling settings and MinSR schedule listed in the tables. The fixed magnetic functions contain no trainable parameters and are excluded from the parameter counts.

We also performed supplementary experiments with four-determinant Real and Complex SlaterNets, using the same hyperparameters as the neural HF references in Table 3. The trainable real parameter counts increase to 18,94418{,}944 and 15,90415{,}904, respectively. Their determinant values are summed directly without independent mixing coefficients. These supplementary architectural controls have training diagnostics separate from the frozen Real–Complex comparisons in Section IV.1.

The Psiformer pair matches the hidden real dimension, depth, determinant count, and attention widths. Complex Psiformer has slightly fewer trainable parameters. Its attention branch also uses a warmup ramp and a cap on the residual root-mean-square amplitude relative to the input, as specified in the code configurations. The benchmark fixes these settings and the number of optimization steps. Hyperparameter-search budgets and total GPU time are not matched.

The independent density and structure-factor evaluation uses the 1818-cell system at nϕ=0,…,4n_{\phi}=0,\ldots,4. The density profiles in Figure 4 and component estimates in Figure 7 use all 393,216 configurations of each state. These estimates use separate Monte Carlo samples from the momentum-space maps in Figure 6. All five flux sectors use training seed 11 and were optimized separately.

Appendix G Charge-order diagnostics

The density maps use the lattice vectors of Section II.1. The Cartesian coordinates follow from 𝒓=(x,y)=u1​𝑳1+u2​𝑳2\bm{r}=(x,y)=u_{1}\bm{L}_{1}+u_{2}\bm{L}_{2}, with 0≤u1,u2<10\leq u_{1},u_{2}<1, so that

xaM=n1​u1+n2​u22,yaM=3​n2​u22.\frac{x}{a_{\mathrm{M}}}=n_{1}u_{1}+\frac{n_{2}u_{2}}{2},\qquad\frac{y}{a_{\mathrm{M}}}=\frac{\sqrt{3}\,n_{2}u_{2}}{2}.

The plotted origin is the cell corner, whereas x∥,x⟂x_{\parallel},x_{\perp} in the magnetic-section construction are measured from the cell center 𝒍\bm{l}. The Jacobian multiplies ρ\rho and its spatial mean ⟨ρ⟩=N/Ω\langle\rho\rangle=N/\Omega by the same factor, leaving the plotted ratio unchanged. We use the six primitive Brillouin-zone corners to probe three-sublattice order,

{±2​𝒈1+𝒈23,±𝒈1+2​𝒈23,±𝒈1−𝒈23}.\left\{\pm\frac{2\bm{g}_{1}+\bm{g}_{2}}{3},\;\pm\frac{\bm{g}_{1}+2\bm{g}_{2}}{3},\;\pm\frac{\bm{g}_{1}-\bm{g}_{2}}{3}\right\}. (33)

G.1 Structure-factor components

We evaluate the decomposition in Equation (23) at each reciprocal vector before averaging over the six vectors in Equation (33). Figure 7 shows the resulting S⁡(K)S(K), Sdisc​(K)S_{\rm disc}(K), and Sconn​(K)S_{\rm conn}(K). At zero field, Complex and Real Psiformer give S⁡(K)=0.707±0.002S(K)=0.707\pm 0.002 and 0.633±0.0010.633\pm 0.001, respectively. Uncertainties are time-block sampling standard errors. The reciprocal-grid differences Δ​Snϕ​(𝒒)\Delta S_{n_{\phi}}(\bm{q}) share the same zero-field estimate. Comparisons between fluxes must retain the covariance from this shared reference.

Complex Psiformer has its largest S⁡(K)S(K) at nϕ=2n_{\phi}=2, with S⁡(K)=1.65±0.003S(K)=1.65\pm 0.003, compared with 0.851±0.0020.851\pm 0.002 for Real Psiformer. Their disconnected contributions are 1.07±0.0031.07\pm 0.003 and 0.301±0.0010.301\pm 0.001, whereas the connected parts are 0.583±0.0010.583\pm 0.001 and 0.549±0.0010.549\pm 0.001. The mean-density contribution accounts for 95.8%95.8\% of the Complex–Real difference in S⁡(K)S(K) at this flux. Real Psiformer has comparable total maxima near nϕ=1n_{\phi}=1 and 44, again with substantial disconnected contributions. The connected Complex values range from 0.5500.550 to 0.6610.661, while the Real values range from 0.5490.549 to 0.6270.627, so the larger total structure factor does not imply larger connected fluctuations. At nϕ=4n_{\phi}=4, the Complex disconnected contribution is only Sdisc​(K)=0.00136±0.000120S_{\rm disc}(K)=0.00136\pm 0.000120, consistent with the suppressed three-sublattice mean-density pattern. These quantities probe the KK star and leave open possible order at other wavevectors or order hidden by symmetry averaging.

For example, equal statistical averaging over the three translated honeycomb charge patterns cancels their mean-density Fourier component at the KK star. Translation changes the phase of this component while leaving its squared magnitude unchanged. The corresponding contribution to S⁡(K)S(K) then enters Sconn​(K)S_{\rm conn}(K). This illustrates how crystalline correlations can survive the loss of a mean-density motif. The present scan does not establish that such averaging occurs in the high-field state.

G.2 Three-sublattice occupation

To compare the 1818-cell densities with the honeycomb motif, we assign every electron to its nearest moiré-potential minimum using the periodic Cartesian distance. The resulting mean well occupation is denoted by nℓn_{\ell}, with ∑ℓ=118nℓ=12\sum_{\ell=1}^{18}n_{\ell}=12. For primitive vectors separated by 60∘60^{\circ}, a well at i​𝒂1+j​𝒂2i\bm{a}_{1}+j\bm{a}_{2} belongs to sublattice s=(i−j)mod3s=(i-j)\bmod 3. We label s=0,1,2s=0,1,2 by A,B,CA,B,C, respectively. Each sublattice contains six wells, and every nearest-neighbor bond connects different sublattices. Let n¯s\bar{n}_{s} be the mean within sublattice ss and n¯=2/3\bar{n}=2/3 the mean over all wells.

We quantify the sublattice pattern through the fraction of the well-to-well occupation variation accounted for by the three sublattice means,

f3=6​∑s=A,B,C(n¯s−n¯)2∑ℓ=118(nℓ−n¯)2.f_{3}=\frac{6\sum_{s=A,B,C}(\bar{n}_{s}-\bar{n})^{2}}{\sum_{\ell=1}^{18}(n_{\ell}-\bar{n})^{2}}.

For nonzero total variation, f3f_{3} ranges from zero to one. It measures three-sublattice modulation but does not specify which sublattices are occupied. We therefore also report dhd_{\rm h}, the root-mean-square deviation of the 18 well occupations from an ideal honeycomb pattern with two occupied sublattices and one empty sublattice. We take the smallest deviation among the three choices of empty sublattice, without rearranging individual wells. Quantum fluctuations and finite localization can yield noninteger occupations even in an ordered state.

Table 6 shows that the Complex state is closest to the ideal honeycomb pattern at nϕ=2n_{\phi}=2, where its sublattice means account for 96.9%96.9\% of the occupation variation. At zero field, its sublattice means are (0.577,0.861,0.562)(0.577,0.861,0.562), without the depleted sublattice characteristic of the honeycomb motif. A larger S⁡(K)S(K) alone therefore does not identify that pattern. At nϕ=4n_{\phi}=4, the Real state is closer to the ideal motif, so the relative agreement at nϕ=2n_{\phi}=2 does not extend across the full scan.

These occupation measures were chosen after examining the flux scan and use the same 393,216 weighted configurations as the density profiles. We report point estimates because uncertainties in f3f_{3} and dhd_{\rm h} require covariances between well occupations, which are unavailable from the archived per-well standard errors.

G.3 Seed dependence in the 2525-cell system

For the incommensurate 5×55\times 5 geometry, we evaluate density anisotropy at the allowed reciprocal-grid points nearest to the three independent MM directions. We take the largest minus the smallest of their disconnected structure-factor values and divide by their mean. This dimensionless ratio measures the variation among the three directions. Across the five independently optimized seeds, its mean and sample standard deviation are 1.82±0.5621.82\pm 0.562 for Complex Psiformer and 1.40±0.5151.40\pm 0.515 for Real Psiformer. Figure 11 shows all individual values. The broad overlap shows that the apparent anisotropy depends on initialization and does not consistently separate the two architectures. The filling 12/2512/25 and allowed reciprocal vectors also differ from the half-filled stripe reference of Ref. [25].
